mockTask.q: A detector flags 5% of benign traffic and catches 99% of attacks. Attacks are 1% of traffic. Roughly what fraction of flags are real attacks?
mockTask.explain: Bayes with base rates: only ~17% of flags are real — the base-rate effect.

notes.title: Describing data, computed
Probability rules
Conditional probability and Bayes
notes.body: Bayes: P(D|+) = P(+|D)·P(D) / P(+). Worked example: 1% of requests are malicious (0.01); the detector catches 99% of malicious and flags 5% of benign. P(+) = 0.99×0.01 + 0.05×0.99 = **0.0594**. So P(malicious | flagged) = 0.0099/0.0594 = **0.167** — only about 1 in 6 flags is real. This is the base-rate effect: with rare events, even good tests produce mostly false positives. Every alert-fatigue argument in operations is Bayes in disguise.

notes.title: Expectation
notes.body: E[X] = Σ x·P(x): the long-run average. Worked example: a retry policy succeeds on attempt 1 with p=0.7, attempt 2 with p=0.2, attempt 3 with p=0.1 (then gives up). Expected attempts = 1×0.7 + 2×0.2 + 3×0.1 = **1.4000000000000001**. Linearity of expectation: E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] even when X,Y are dependent — the workhorse for analyzing total cost, total latency, total errors across components without modeling their joint distribution.

notes.title: The binomial distribution, computed
notes.body: P(X=k) = C(n,k)·p^k·(1−p)^(n−k). Worked example: 10 requests, each fails independently with p=0.5 (a coin). P(exactly 3 fail) = C(10,3)×0.5^3×0.5^7 = 120×0.5^10 = **0.1172**. Sanity: probabilities over k=0..10 sum to 1.000000 = 1 ✓. Use the binomial for 'k of n independent trials' questions — canary failures, bit errors, A/B conversions.

cards.front: State De Morgan's law for AND.
cards.back: NOT (p AND q) = (NOT p) OR (NOT q) — verified on all 4 rows.

cards.front: State De Morgan's law for OR.
cards.back: NOT (p OR q) = (NOT p) AND (NOT q).

cards.front: Define p -> q without using ->.
cards.back: (NOT p) OR q. Only false when p=T, q=F.

cards.front: What is the contrapositive of p -> q?
cards.back: (NOT q) -> (NOT p) — logically equivalent to the original.

cards.front: Is the converse of p -> q equivalent to p -> q?
cards.back: No. Counterexample: p=T, q=F makes p->q false but q->p true.

cards.front: Absorption law?
cards.back: p OR (p AND q) = p; p AND (p OR q) = p.

cards.front: What does EXISTS x, P(x) require over a finite domain?
cards.back: At least one domain element making P true — a single witness.

cards.front: What does FORALL x, P(x) require?
cards.back: Every domain element makes P true — one counterexample falsifies it.

cards.back: a — factor to a AND (b OR NOT b) = a AND T.

notes.title: Propositions and truth values
Truth tables, computed by enumeration
De Morgan's laws, verified by brute force
notes.body: De Morgan's laws: `NOT (p AND q)` equals `(NOT p) OR (NOT q)`, and `NOT (p OR q)` equals `(NOT p) AND (NOT q)`. Worked verification: checking all 4 assignments of (p,q) in Python, every row agrees — **True**. This is the law behind simplifying negated conditions: `NOT (admin AND active)` becomes `NOT admin OR NOT active`. In code and in firewall/policy rules, pushing NOT inward with De Morgan turns an unreadable negated conjunction into a plain disjunction.

notes.title: Implication and the contrapositive
notes.body: `p -> q` (if p then q) is logically equivalent to its contrapositive `(NOT q) -> (NOT p)`. Worked verification: all 4 assignments agree — **True**. The converse `q -> p` is NOT equivalent (check p=T,q=F: implication false, converse true). Practical use: to prove 'if the build passes then tests ran', prove the contrapositive 'if tests did not run then the build fails' — often the easier direction. Confusing implication with converse is one of the most common logic errors in specifications.

notes.title: Predicate logic over finite domains
notes.body: Predicates add quantifiers: `FORALL x, P(x)` and `EXISTS x, P(x)`. Over a finite domain you can evaluate them by enumeration. Worked example: domain = {2, 3, 4}, statement `EXISTS x, x is prime AND x > 3`. Check: x=2 (prime, not >3, fails), x=3 (prime, not >3, fails), x=4 (not prime, fails). No witness exists, so the statement is **false**. Change `>3` to `>=3`: x=3 is prime and >= 3, so the statement becomes **true**. Existence claims need exactly one witness; universal claims need every case. This discipline maps directly onto testing: 'there exists an input that crashes' vs 'for all inputs it terminates'.

cards.front: What are the four golden signals?
cards.back: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation — the minimum dashboard for any service. In an interview, reach for them first: ‘I’d check the four golden signals’ is the SRE equivalent of ‘let me reproduce it.’

cards.front: SLI vs SLO vs SLA?
cards.back: SLI: the measured indicator (e.g. successful requests / total). SLO: the target on the SLI (99.9% over 30 days). SLA: the contract with consequences. The interview line: ‘SLIs are facts, SLOs are promises, SLAs are contracts.’

cards.front: How do error budgets govern releases?
cards.back: Budget remaining → ship freely. Budget exhausted → freeze risky changes until reliability recovers. It replaces arguments about ‘are we reliable enough’ with arithmetic — the interview line: ‘the budget turns reliability into a joint product decision.’

cards.front: How do you explain burn-rate alerting?
cards.back: Instead of alerting on raw error counts, alert on how fast the error budget is being consumed relative to the SLO window: fast-burn (page now) vs slow-burn (ticket). Multiwindow alerts catch both without paging on blips.

cards.front: How do you measure SLIs with Prometheus?
cards.back: Counters for requests and errors (rate over windows), histograms/summaries for latency percentiles, recording rules to precompute SLI ratios, and burn-rate alert rules on top. The interview line: ‘the SLI is a PromQL expression with an SLO attached.’

cards.front: How do you size an error budget on a whiteboard?
cards.back: 99.9% over 30 days → 0.1% of 43,200 minutes = 43.2 minutes of total allowed badness per month. Say it as policy: 'our budget is roughly one real incident a month — while budget remains we ship, when it's spent we harden.' The interview line: 'budgets are arithmetic, not vibes.'

cards.front: How do you pick the right SLI for a service?
cards.back: Measure what the user feels: request success ratio and latency percentiles for serving paths — not CPU. The interview line: ‘the SLI is the user’s experience expressed as a number.’

cards.front: What makes an SLO credible in an interview answer?
cards.back: Tied to user impact, with the error-budget policy attached: who decides when the budget burns, and what stops. The interview line: ‘an SLO without a budget policy is a wish.’

cards.front: A latency SLI in Prometheus is typically built from:
cards.back: **Histogram buckets — enabling accurate percentile computation over windows** — Histograms preserve the distribution: any percentile over any window is computable.

cards.front: Burn-rate alerting’s advantage over static error thresholds is:
cards.back: **It measures budget consumption relative to the SLO — paging only when the objective is actually at risk** — Thresholds don’t know your SLO; burn rate ties paging directly to objective risk.

cards.front: When the error budget is exhausted, the correct policy is:
cards.back: **Freeze or slow risky releases until the budget recovers** — The budget is the agreed tradeoff dial: spending it all means reliability work comes first.

cards.front: An error budget is:
cards.back: **1 − SLO: the allowed failure rate, spent deliberately on releases and risk** — 99.9% SLO → 0.1% budget: reliability as a spendable resource balancing velocity and stability.

notes.body: Preparation only — this course confers no certificate, and rehearsing SLO math is not the same as carrying a production error budget. Real budgets are negotiated with product and customers, and real paging policies are tuned against months of alert history you don't have yet. What this module does give you is the interview's language — SLIs are facts, SLOs are promises, SLAs are contracts — and the arithmetic to defend them on a whiteboard. Vendor specifics follow vendor documentation, which changes; check the linked sources as of their retrieval dates.

notes.title: Worked example: A latency SLI in Prometheus is typically built from:
notes.body:
**Problem.** A latency SLI in Prometheus is typically built from:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Histogram buckets — enabling accurate percentile computation over windows
- **Why:** Histograms preserve the distribution: any percentile over any window is computable.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Histograms preserve the distribution: any percentile over any window is computable.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

cards.front: Walk the incident lifecycle.
cards.back: Detect (alerts, user reports) → respond (declare, assemble, IC takes command) → mitigate (stop the bleeding — rollback, shed load) → resolve → learn (blameless postmortem). The interview line: ‘mitigate first, understand second.’

cards.front: What are the incident command roles?
cards.back: Incident Commander (decides, coordinates — doesn’t debug), Communications (status updates, stakeholders), Scribe (timeline), plus subject-matter experts debugging. The IC’s job is the incident, not the keyboard.

cards.front: How do you classify incident severity in an SRE interview?
cards.back: SEV levels by user impact and urgency: SEV-1 (critical — core function down, all hands), SEV-2 (major degradation), SEV-3 (minor, limited blast radius). Severity is impact; priority is scheduling. The interview line: ‘severity describes the fire, not who fights it.’

cards.front: How do you communicate during an outage?
cards.back: One channel (#incident), regular cadence (every 15–30 min even with ‘no update’), impact-first language (who’s affected, what we’re doing, when’s the next update), and a single comms owner. The interview line: ‘silence during an outage is a second outage.’

cards.front: What makes a postmortem blameless and useful?
cards.back: Blameless: systems and process, never people — or nobody will write honestly. Structure: timeline, impact, root causes (plural — ‘five whys’), action items with owners and dates. The interview line: ‘the postmortem’s value is the action items, not the document.’

cards.front: When do you escalate an incident's severity?
cards.back: When the impact scope grows: more users affected, a longer blast radius, or the mitigation isn't working. Severity follows impact, not effort — and the paging policy decides who the escalation wakes. The interview line: 'I escalate on impact, early; downgrading is cheaper than discovering the blast radius at the postmortem.'

cards.front: How do you run the first five minutes of an incident?
cards.back: Declare, take command, freeze the scope: who is impacted, what is the mitigation hypothesis, who owns comms. The interview line: ‘the first five minutes buy the next fifty.’

cards.front: What goes in a status update during an outage?
cards.back: Impact (who is affected), what is known, what is being done, when the next update lands — even if it is ‘no change.’ The interview line: ‘silence during an outage is a second incident.’

cards.front: An ML system design that only covers the model is weak because:
cards.back: **Production value lives in data, serving, and monitoring — the model is one piece** — Most ML failures are systems failures: skew, drift, latency — not the algorithm.

cards.front: Blameless postmortems work because:
cards.back: **Removing blame gets honest timelines — people report what really happened** — Honest data requires psychological safety; blame produces cover stories instead of root causes.

cards.front: Status updates during an outage should lead with:
cards.back: **Customer impact: who’s affected and what’s being done** — Stakeholders need impact and next-update time; deep technical detail follows for those who need it.

cards.front: Severity vs priority differ in that:
cards.back: **Severity = impact on users; priority = order of fixing (business decision)** — A severe bug in a deprecated feature can be low priority; a trivial bug blocking launch is high priority.

notes.body:
**Problem.** An ML system design that only covers the model is weak because:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Production value lives in data, serving, and monitoring — the model is one piece
- **Why:** Most ML failures are systems failures: skew, drift, latency — not the algorithm.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Most ML failures are systems failures: skew, drift, latency — not the algorithm.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

cards.front: Metrics, logs, traces — the three pillars in an SRE interview?
cards.back: Metrics: numbers over time (alerts, trends). Logs: discrete events with context (the why). Traces: request journeys across services (the where). The interview line: ‘metrics tell me something’s wrong, traces show me where, logs tell me why.’

cards.front: What are the four golden signals?
cards.back: Latency, traffic, errors, saturation — the minimum dashboard for any service. In an interview, reach for them first: ‘I’d check the four golden signals’ is the SRE equivalent of ‘let me reproduce it.’

cards.front: USE vs RED methods?
cards.back: USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for resources — ‘is the box healthy.’ RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) for services — ‘is the service healthy.’ In an interview, name which lens fits: debugging a host → USE; debugging an API → RED.

cards.front: Why alert on symptoms, not causes?
cards.back: Users feel symptoms (latency, error rate); causes are legion and change. Symptom alerts (burn rate, golden signals) page on user impact; cause-based alerts (‘disk 90%’) page on things that may not matter — alert fatigue follows.

cards.front: What makes a dashboard that ‘answers questions’?
cards.back: Golden signals up top, drill-down from symptom to cause, time-range comparisons, and annotations for deploys — organized by the questions on-call asks at 3am, not by data source. The interview line: ‘a dashboard is a UI for incident questions.’

cards.front: How do you decide what belongs in logs vs metrics?
cards.back: Metrics get the countable and the alertable — rates, latencies, saturations with bounded labels. Logs get the discrete and the contextual — errors with request IDs, decisions, anomalies to investigate. Traces get the cross-service journey. The interview line: 'if I'd page on it, it's a metric; if I'd investigate with it, it's a log.'

cards.front: How do you explain cardinality discipline in metrics?
cards.back: Bounded label values only: high-cardinality labels (user IDs, request IDs) explode storage and cost. The interview line: ‘labels are dimensions, not databases.’

cards.front: What makes an alert actionable?
cards.back: It fires on a symptom tied to an SLO, names the runbook, and pages only when a human must act now. The interview line: ‘an alert without an action is a notification.’

cards.front: Putting user_id in a Prometheus label is dangerous because:
cards.back: **Each unique value creates a new time series — cardinality explosion** — Unbounded label values × metrics = millions of series; memory and query costs follow.

cards.front: Deploy annotations on dashboards help because:
cards.back: **They correlate behavior changes with releases — the first suspect in any regression** — ‘What changed?’ is the first incident question; annotations answer it at a glance.

cards.front: Alerting on symptoms means paging when:
cards.back: **User-facing indicators (latency/errors) breach SLO — regardless of underlying cause** — Pages should mean user impact; cause metrics are for dashboards and diagnosis, not paging.

cards.front: The RED method suits:
cards.back: **Request-driven services: rate, errors, duration** — RED describes service behavior from the requester’s view; USE describes resource internals.

cards.front: How do you forecast demand for capacity planning?
cards.back: Historical growth rates plus known events (launches, seasonality, marketing), expressed as ranges not points, translated through the capacity model (requests → resources). The interview line: ‘forecasts are ranges with assumptions, reviewed on a cadence.’

cards.front: k6 vs JMeter — how do you compare them?
cards.back: k6: JS-scripted, developer-friendly, great for CI-integrated load tests with thresholds as gates. JMeter: GUI-driven, mature, huge protocol support, heavier. The interview line: ‘k6 for code-reviewed load tests in the pipeline; JMeter where the team already lives in it.’

cards.front: HPA vs VPA?
cards.back: HPA: more pods when load rises (horizontal — the cloud-native default). VPA: bigger pods (vertical — for workloads that can’t scale out, needs restarts). The interview caveat: autoscaling isn’t instant — cold starts and scaling lag mean you still need headroom.

cards.front: What’s the utilization wall?
cards.back: Latency degrades nonlinearly as utilization approaches 100% (queueing theory): a system at 90%+ has no headroom for bursts — the ‘wall’ where small load increases cause large latency spikes. The interview line: ‘I plan headroom against the wall, not against the average.’

cards.front: How do you use Little’s Law in capacity planning?
cards.back: L = λW: average items in the system equals arrival rate times average time in system. It turns a latency SLO into a concurrency requirement — and a concurrency limit into a queueing prediction. The interview line: ‘Little’s Law converts between the rate I provision for and the latency I promise.’

cards.front: What do you load-test before a launch, and what makes the test a gate?
cards.back: The forecast peak (at 1.5× for margin), a soak run for leaks, and a spike run for autoscaling lag — each with pass/fail thresholds written before the test runs. A threshold decided after the results is decoration; decided before, it's a gate. The interview line: 'the load test is a hypothesis test on my capacity model.'

cards.front: How do you discuss headroom in capacity planning?
cards.back: Provision for peak plus margin (the forecast at 1.5×), because the utilization wall punishes 90%+ — latency degrades nonlinearly. The interview line: ‘headroom is the price of the p99.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in autoscaling lag?
cards.back: Metrics delay plus pod-startup time means autoscaling reacts late to spikes — pre-warming and an over-provisioned buffer cover the gap. The interview line: ‘autoscaling is reactive; the spike doesn’t wait.’

cards.front: Spot instances fit batch workloads because:
cards.back: **Interruption-tolerant work buys spare capacity at deep discounts** — Price follows preemptibility; batch work that checkpoints doesn’t care.

cards.front: Eager loading fixes N+1 by:
cards.back: **Fetching related rows in bulk (JOIN or batched query) instead of one query per parent** — One bulk fetch replaces N per-row queries; round trips collapse from N+1 to ~2.

cards.front: Running a service at 95% CPU is risky because:
cards.back: **Queueing effects make latency spike nonlinearly near saturation — no burst headroom** — Near 100% utilization, tiny load increases produce huge queueing delays.

cards.front: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler reacts to load by:
cards.back: **Adding more pod replicas** — HPA scales replica count on metrics; VPA resizes individual pods.

cards.front: How do you design for multi-region in an interview?
cards.back: Active-passive (one serves, one stands by) vs active-active (both serve — needs conflict resolution); data replication with RPO/RTO stated; DNS or anycast failover; and the honest cost: complexity and consistency tradeoffs multiply. The interview line: ‘multi-region is a business decision with an engineering price.’

cards.front: What is backpressure, and where do you put it?
cards.back: When consumers are slower than producers, pressure must go somewhere: bounded queues that block/shed, reactive streams with demand signaling, or Kafka consumer-lag alerting. The interview point: an unbounded queue is a deferred outage.

cards.front: How do caching layers behave under failure?
cards.back: Cache stampedes on cold start, thundering herd on hot-key expiry, and the deadly combo: cache down → DB overload → cascading failure. Defenses: request coalescing, staggered TTLs, circuit breakers, and graceful degradation (serve stale while revalidating).

cards.front: What’s load shedding, and when do you use it?
cards.back: Deliberately dropping low-priority work to protect the core: priority queues, shedding non-critical traffic at the edge, degrading features gracefully. The interview line: ‘shedding is a choice — uncontrolled collapse is not.’

cards.front: What’s the standard system-design walkthrough?
cards.back: Requirements → estimation → API → data model → happy-path design → scaling/bottlenecks → failure modes → tradeoffs summary. Drive with questions, think aloud, and treat the interviewer as a collaborator, not an examiner.

cards.front: How do you defend a caching choice in a design round?
cards.back: Name what you cache and why, the invalidation story, and the failure story: stampede on cold start, thundering herd on hot-key expiry, and what happens when the cache itself dies (stale-while-revalidate, circuit breaker). The interview line: 'caching is a tradeoff with an invalidation plan, not a speedup.'

cards.front: How do you design a health-check strategy in a design round?
cards.back: Layered: liveness (restart me) vs readiness (don’t send traffic yet), with dependency checks that fail fast. The interview line: ‘health checks are the system’s honesty about itself.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in graceful degradation?
cards.back: Defined fallback tiers: full → reduced (cached/stale) → static — each with its trigger condition. The interview line: ‘degradation designed beats degradation discovered.’

cards.front: In a design round, the interviewer is best treated as:
cards.back: **A collaborator — ask questions, incorporate feedback, design together** — Design rounds simulate real design work: collaborative, iterative, tradeoff-driven.

cards.front: Load shedding differs from a cascading failure in that it’s:
cards.back: **Deliberate and prioritized — you choose what degrades instead of everything failing** — Controlled degradation preserves the critical path; cascades take everything down.

cards.front: Serving stale cache during an origin outage is:
cards.back: **Graceful degradation — slightly old data beats no data** — Stale-while-revalidate as a failure mode keeps the product usable while the origin recovers.

cards.front: A bounded queue with a drop-or-block policy implements:
cards.back: **Backpressure — the producer feels the consumer’s slowness** — Bounded buffers propagate slowness upstream instead of growing memory until collapse.

cards.front: How do you prep for SRE mock rounds (incident, metrics/SLO, system design)?
cards.back: Incident: run the lifecycle aloud (declare, mitigate first, comms cadence). Metrics/SLO: define SLIs, do the budget math, name burn-rate alerting. Design: requirements → estimation → HA design → failure modes. The interview line: ‘each round has a shape — I rehearse the shape.’

cards.front: How do behavioral rounds differ for SREs?
cards.back: They probe ownership under pressure: on-call stories, incident decisions, disagreements about risk, and learning from outages — all STAR, all blameless. The interview line: ‘SRE behavioral rounds grade how I act when the pager fires.’

cards.front: How do you score yourself against an interview rubric?
cards.back: Fixed axes per round type: correctness, complexity analysis, communication, time management, tradeoffs named. Score honestly after every mock; the rubric turns feelings into data. The interview line: ‘I grade myself the way they’ll grade me.’

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?
cards.back: Stop learning new topics; redrill weak patterns from your debrief log, run full timed mocks, fix sleep, and rehearse your story bank aloud. The taper converts knowledge into performance — cramming new material now only adds noise.

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Mock incident round'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: What's on your 48-hour pre-interview checklist?
cards.back: Logistics confirmed, sleep protected, story bank rehearsed aloud, the two weakest round shapes redrilled once more — and explicitly: no new topics. The checklist converts preparation into performance; cramming converts it into noise. The interview line: 'the last 48 hours are about the performer, not the material.'

cards.front: How do you prep the incident round specifically?
cards.back: Run the lifecycle aloud on a past outage: declare, mitigate first, comms cadence — blameless language throughout. The interview line: ‘the incident round grades command, not debugging.’

cards.front: What does the SRE rubric’s ‘judgment under pressure’ axis mean?
cards.back: Decisions with incomplete data: when you mitigated vs kept digging, when you escalated, what you communicated. The interview line: ‘judgment is visible in the tradeoffs you name.’

cards.front: The taper period’s rule is:
cards.back: **No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest** — Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

cards.front: Rubric scoring beats gut feeling because:
cards.back: **It makes weaknesses comparable across mocks — triage needs data** — You can’t triage what you haven’t measured.

cards.front: An SRE behavioral answer should emphasize:
cards.back: **Decisions under pressure, communication, and systemic learning** — Reliability is a team sport; the graded behaviors are judgment and coordination.

cards.front: Rehearsing each round’s ‘shape’ helps because:
cards.back: **Interviews grade method under pressure — the shape is the method, made automatic** — Automatic structure frees mental budget for the novel parts of the problem.

cards.front: What’s the case for trunk-based development?
cards.back: Small, frequent merges to main behind feature flags: integration pain drops with merge frequency, main stays releasable, and long-lived branch divergence dies. The interview line: ‘branches are inventory — trunk-based keeps inventory near zero.’

cards.front: What belongs in CI stages, and in what order?
cards.back: Fast-first: lint and unit tests (minutes), then build, integration tests, security scans, artifact publish. The interview line: ‘fail fast and cheap — a 40-minute pipeline that fails at minute 39 teaches nothing quickly.’

cards.front: Why do artifacts and registries matter?
cards.back: Build once, promote the same immutable artifact through environments — registries (container/image, package) make ‘what’s running where’ answerable. The interview line: ‘if you rebuild per environment, you didn’t test what you shipped.’

cards.front: Blue-green vs canary vs rolling?
cards.back: Blue-green: two full environments, instant cutover and rollback — costs double capacity. Canary: new version to a small % first, promote on metrics — safest for risky changes. Rolling: gradual replacement — simplest, slowest rollback. Choose by blast-radius tolerance.

cards.front: What does pipeline-as-code buy you?
cards.back: The pipeline is versioned, reviewed, and reproducible like the app: workflow files in the repo, changes via PR, history in git. The interview line: ‘if the pipeline isn’t in version control, it’s folklore.’

cards.front: How do you keep a 40-minute pipeline from failing at minute 39?
cards.back: Order stages fail-fast: lint and unit tests in the first minutes, then build, integration, scans, publish. Fast, cheap failures first; slow, expensive verification only for code that earned it. The interview line: 'fail fast and cheap — a 40-minute pipeline that fails at minute 39 teaches nothing quickly.'

cards.front: How do you discuss deployment freezes in an interview?
cards.back: Change moratoriums around critical periods (holidays, launches) with a defined exception process — reliability as policy. The interview line: ‘freezes are the error budget made calendar.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in artifact promotion?
cards.back: The same immutable artifact moves dev → staging → prod; only config changes per environment. The interview line: ‘promote the artifact, not a rebuild.’

cards.front: The rollback-vs-fix-forward decision hinges on:
cards.back: **Blast radius and diagnosis confidence — big blast or uncertain cause means roll back** — Uncertain cause + user impact = roll back first, understand second.

cards.front: Storing CI configuration in the repo enables:
cards.back: **Review, versioning, and reproducibility of the pipeline itself** — Pipeline changes get the same rigor as code changes: PRs, history, rollback.

cards.front: Canary deployment’s defining feature is:
cards.back: **Releasing to a small subset first and promoting based on observed metrics** — Progressive exposure with metric gates: problems hit 1% before 100%.

cards.front: Promoting the same immutable artifact through environments ensures:
cards.back: **What you tested is what you ship — no rebuild skew between staging and prod** — Rebuilding per environment invalidates testing; immutable artifacts preserve it.

cards.front: Declarative vs imperative infrastructure?
cards.back: Declarative: state the desired end state, the tool converges (Terraform, K8s manifests) — idempotent and auditable. Imperative: script the steps — flexible but order-dependent and drift-prone. The interview line: ‘I declare the destination; the tool figures out the route.’

cards.front: How do you explain Terraform’s workflow?
cards.back: Write declarative HCL, plan to preview the diff, apply to converge. State tracks reality (remote backend, locking!); modules compose reusable units. The interview traps: state drift, and why plan-before-apply is non-negotiable.

cards.front: How do you discuss Terraform state tradeoffs?
cards.back: Remote state with locking (no local state files on a team), state per environment to bound blast radius, and never hand-editing state — import or taint instead. The tradeoff: finer state splits mean safer applies but more orchestration. The interview line: ‘state is the map of reality; guard it like production data.’

cards.front: How do you structure Terraform modules and composition?
cards.back: Small composable modules (one concern each: network, compute, data), composed in environment roots with explicit inputs — no deep nesting. The interview line: ‘modules are functions; roots are the programs that call them.’

cards.front: What is infrastructure drift, and how do you fight it?
cards.back: Reality diverging from declared config (manual console clicks). Detection: scheduled plan runs that alert on diffs; prevention: make the console read-only, everything through code. The interview line: ‘drift is how outages hide.’

cards.front: Why is 'plan-before-apply' non-negotiable?
cards.back: The plan is the diff between declared and actual — it's the review, the blast-radius estimate, and the last chance to catch a typo that deletes the database. Applying blind is clicking 'yes' on a dialog you didn't read. The interview line: 'the plan is the change's résumé; I read résumés before hiring.'

cards.front: How do you discuss secret handling in IaC?
cards.back: Never in state files or repos in plaintext: secret managers with dynamic references, state encrypted at rest. The interview line: ‘the state file is a secret — treat it like one.’

cards.front: What makes a Terraform module reusable?
cards.back: Small scope, documented inputs and outputs, no hardcoded environment values — composition in environment roots. The interview line: ‘modules are libraries; roots are applications.’

cards.front: Enforcing policy at plan time (vs after deploy) is better because:
cards.back: **Violations are blocked before they exist — prevention beats detection** — Shift-left for governance: the bad change never reaches the cloud.

cards.front: The primary defense against drift is:
cards.back: **Everything through code + scheduled plan/detect cycles** — If all changes flow through IaC, reality can’t silently diverge.

cards.front: Deep module nesting is an anti-pattern because:
cards.back: **Inputs tunnel through layers opaquely — debugging and reuse both suffer** — Flat composition keeps the dependency graph legible; nesting hides it.

cards.front: React context is a poor state manager for high-churn state because:
cards.back: **Every consumer re-renders on any context value change** — Context has no selectors: one value change re-renders all consumers regardless of what they use.

quiz.explain: Context has no selectors: one value change re-renders all consumers regardless of what they use.

quiz.q: Two engineers applying Terraform at once is safe only with:
choices: Remote state with locking — concurrent applies can't corrupt state
quiz.explain: Locking serializes applies; without it, state corrupts — the Hands-on procedure step 3.

quiz.q: A scheduled 'terraform plan' that alerts on diffs is:
choices: Drift detection — reality diverging from declared config gets caught
quiz.explain: Detection is the scheduled plan run; prevention is everything-through-code — the Concepts.

quiz.q: Environment roots composing small modules with explicit inputs beat deep nesting because:
choices: Inputs stay visible — deep nesting tunnels them opaquely and both debugging and reuse suffer
quiz.explain: Flat composition keeps the dependency graph legible — 'modules are functions; roots are the programs.'

quiz.q: Policy-as-code at plan time beats post-deploy auditing because:
choices: Violations are blocked before they exist — prevention beats detection
quiz.explain: The bad change never reaches the cloud — the Hands-on procedure step 5.

quiz.q: Making the cloud console read-only for humans prevents drift by:
choices: Forcing every change through code, so reality can't silently diverge
quiz.explain: If all changes flow through IaC, the declared state stays the actual state — the Project brief.

quiz.q: Storing Terraform state on a laptop is wrong because:
choices: State is shared truth — it needs a remote backend with locking, versioning, and access control
quiz.explain: State tracks reality for the whole team; a laptop is a single point of loss and conflict — the Concepts.

cards.front: How do Docker layers affect your Dockerfile?
cards.back: Each instruction is a cached layer: order matters — put slow-changing steps (dependency install) before fast-changing ones (code copy) to maximize cache hits. Multi-stage builds keep runtime images small: build in one stage, ship only artifacts.

cards.front: What’s tagging discipline for container registries?
cards.back: Immutable tags per build (git SHA), floating tags (latest) only for convenience — never deploy ‘latest’ to prod. The interview line: ‘mutable tags make ‘what’s running?’ unanswerable.’

cards.front: The Kubernetes objects you must know cold?
cards.back: Pod (smallest unit), Deployment (declarative replicas + rolling updates), Service (stable networking), Ingress (external HTTP routing), ConfigMap/Secret (config separation), PersistentVolume for state. The interview walk: ‘my app runs as a Deployment behind a Service, exposed via Ingress.’

cards.front: How do Deployments, Services, and Ingress fit together?
cards.back: Deployment: declares the desired pods and rolling-update strategy. Service: stable internal endpoint selecting those pods. Ingress: external HTTP routing (host/path → service). The interview line: ‘three layers: run it, find it, expose it.’

cards.front: How do you handle config vs secrets in Kubernetes?
cards.back: ConfigMaps for non-sensitive config, Secrets for sensitive (base64-encoded, not encrypted by default — use external secret managers or encryption at rest for real protection). Mount as env or files; never bake into images. The interview line: ‘config travels with the deployment, not the image.’

cards.front: How do you shrink a 1.2 GB container image?
cards.back: Multi-stage build (ship only runtime artifacts), minimal base image, dependencies before code copy for cache efficiency, and audit what's inside — build tools and caches don't sail to prod. Smaller images pull faster, scan faster, and shrink the attack surface. The interview line: 'the image should contain the app, not the workshop.'

cards.front: How do you discuss pod resource requests vs limits?
cards.back: Requests: the scheduler’s guarantee (bin-packing basis). Limits: the kill threshold (OOMKilled). Set requests from measured p95, limits with headroom. The interview line: ‘requests are reservations; limits are the ceiling.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in liveness vs readiness probes?
cards.back: Liveness: restart the stuck container. Readiness: hold traffic during startup or dependency outages. Wrong probe, cascading restarts. The interview line: ‘the probes are the orchestrator’s senses — calibrate them.’

cards.front: Helm’s ‘values’ mechanism lets you:
cards.back: **Deploy the same chart across environments with different configuration** — One chart, many values files: dev/staging/prod differ by values, not by forked manifests.

cards.front: Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded, which means:
cards.back: **They’re obfuscated, not encrypted — anyone with API access can decode them** — Base64 is encoding, not encryption: etcd encryption or external secret managers provide real protection.

cards.front: An Ingress resource needs an Ingress controller because:
cards.back: **Ingress is just config — the controller is the actual proxy implementing the routing** — The resource declares intent; the controller (nginx, traefik) does the work.

cards.front: A Kubernetes Service provides:
cards.back: **Stable networking (DNS + load balancing) for a set of pods** — Pods are ephemeral; the Service gives them a stable virtual IP and DNS name.

**Problem.** Helm’s ‘values’ mechanism lets you:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Deploy the same chart across environments with different configuration

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

cards.front: How do you read logs under pressure?
cards.back: Filter ruthlessly: time window around the incident, the failing service first, errors before info, one clear signal at a time. Correlate with deploys and metric spikes. The interview line: ‘I narrow before I read — logs are guilty until filtered innocent.’

cards.front: How do you actually run five whys on a system?
cards.back: Start from the symptom and ask ‘why’ iteratively, following evidence (logs, metrics, deploys) not hunches — until you reach a process/systemic cause with an action item. The discipline: every ‘why’ needs data, and the fifth why usually points at a missing guardrail.

cards.front: How do you debug network issues methodically?
cards.back: Layer by layer: DNS resolves? (dig/nslookup) TCP connects? (curl -v, telnet) TLS handshakes? (openssl s_client) HTTP responds? Each layer’s test isolates the fault — the interview line: ‘I bisect the stack instead of guessing.’

cards.front: What Kubernetes failure modes must you know?
cards.back: CrashLoopBackOff (bad image/config, failing probes), ImagePullBackOff (registry/auth), OOMKilled (limits vs reality), Pending (no schedulable node/resources), probe misconfiguration (killing healthy pods). The interview line: ‘kubectl describe tells you the story; events are the narrator.’

cards.front: Why do interviewers grade ‘thinking aloud’ in troubleshooting rounds?
cards.back: Because silent debugging is unscoreable: narrating hypotheses, what each command tests, and what the output means lets them evaluate your method. The structure: hypothesis → test → observe → update, said out loud.

cards.front: What's your first move when the dashboard is red but nobody knows why?
cards.back: Ask 'what changed?' — check deploy annotations and recent deploys before touching anything. Most production mysteries are deployments in disguise, and the answer is usually in the last hour's timeline. The interview line: 'I investigate the timeline before I investigate the system.'

cards.front: How do you discuss the ‘what changed?’ first move?
cards.back: Deploys, config, traffic, and infra changes in the incident window — most production surprises are changes wearing a costume. The interview line: ‘the timeline of changes is the first log I read.’

cards.front: What makes a troubleshooting hypothesis good?
cards.back: Falsifiable and cheap to test: one command that rules something out. The interview line: ‘debug by elimination, not by inspiration.’

cards.front: Narrating while troubleshooting helps the interviewer assess:
cards.back: **Your diagnostic method — hypotheses, tests, and how you update on evidence** — Method is what’s graded; narration makes the invisible visible.

cards.front: CrashLoopBackOff most often means:
cards.back: **The container starts then exits — bad command, missing config, or failing startup probe** — The kubelet keeps retrying a container that can’t stay alive; describe/events reveal why it dies.

cards.front: curl -v failing at ‘Could not resolve host’ means:
cards.back: **DNS failure — the name never became an IP** — Resolution happens before any connection: the fault is in DNS, not the server.

cards.front: Five whys stops being useful when:
cards.back: **Answers become speculation without evidence — each why needs data** — Whys without evidence are storytelling; the method works when each level is grounded in telemetry.

cards.front: What does a good platform-build scaffold include?
cards.back: Repo layout (app + infra + pipeline), VPC via Terraform, cluster bootstrap scripted, CI pipeline, GitOps deploy — each piece documented as a deliverable. The interview line: ‘the scaffold is the platform’s first impression.’

cards.front: What is a ‘paved road’ in platform engineering?
cards.back: The blessed, supported path: golden-path templates, standard pipelines, and defaults that make the right thing the easy thing. Teams can leave the road, but then they own the maintenance. The interview line: ‘a paved road is opinionated infrastructure with an escape hatch.’

cards.front: What is GitOps, concretely?
cards.back: Git as the single source of truth for desired state; an agent (Argo CD/Flux) continuously reconciles the cluster to it. Pull-based, auditable, self-healing: drift gets reverted automatically, and every change is a git commit.

cards.front: Why is documentation a deliverable in platform work?
cards.back: Because platforms have customers: runbooks, ADRs, and onboarding docs are the API of the platform team. The interview line: ‘undocumented automation is a ticket queue with extra steps.’

notes.title: Worked example: An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) captures:
notes.body:
**Problem.** An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) captures:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** The decision, its context, alternatives considered, and consequences — why, not just what
- **Why:** Future-you needs the reasoning, not just the outcome; ADRs preserve the why.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Future-you needs the reasoning, not just the outcome; ADRs preserve the why.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

cards.front: How do you handle DevOps mock rounds (pipeline design, live troubleshooting)?
cards.back: Pipeline design: stages in order, artifact promotion, rollback story. Live troubleshooting: hypothesis → test → observe, narrated, time-boxed. The interview line: ‘design shows judgment; troubleshooting shows method.’

cards.front: How do behavioral rounds differ for DevOps roles?
cards.back: They probe ownership under pressure: on-call stories, incident decisions, disagreements about risk and automation, and learning from outages — all STAR, all blameless. The interview line: ‘DevOps behavioral rounds grade how I act when the pager fires.’

cards.front: What’s the STAR structure, and why does it work for behavioral rounds?
cards.back: Situation (2 sentences of context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what YOU did — the bulk), Result (measurable outcome + lesson). It works because interviewers score evidence of behavior, and STAR forces a complete evidence unit.

cards.front: What questions should you ask the interviewer?
cards.back: Ones that reveal the job’s reality: ‘what does success look like in 6 months?’, ‘what’s the hardest technical problem the team faces?’, ‘how are on-call and incidents handled?’, ‘why is this role open?’ Never ask what the website answers.

cards.front: How do you handle offer and negotiation basics?
cards.back: Know your market range from data (levels.fyi, peers), let them anchor first when possible, negotiate the whole package (base, equity, bonus, start date) — never just base salary — and get everything in writing. The interview line: ‘I negotiate once, informed and in good faith.’

cards.front: How do you answer 'tell me about a disagreement with a teammate'?
cards.back: STAR with the conflict as the situation: what each side wanted, the data or principle that decided it, what you actually did (listened, proposed, conceded or persuaded), and the result — including what you'd do differently. Blameless, specific, and about the work. The interview line: 'disagreements are design reviews with feelings; I treat them that way.'

cards.front: How do you prep the live-troubleshooting mock?
cards.back: Narrate hypotheses, test cheaply, read the timeline of changes — thinking aloud is the scored skill. The interview line: ‘silent debugging is unscoreable.’

cards.front: What do you ask a DevOps interviewer that scores?
cards.back: On-call reality (frequency, toil), deployment confidence, and what breaks most — questions that reveal the job’s truth. The interview line: ‘ask about the pager before you sign up for it.’

cards.front: Negotiating only base salary is weak because:
cards.back: **Total compensation includes equity, bonus, and benefits — often larger than base deltas** — The package is the number; single-dimension negotiation leaves money unclaimed.

cards.front: The strongest interviewer question reveals:
cards.back: **The role’s reality: success criteria, hard problems, team health** — You’re interviewing them too: these answers predict your actual day-to-day.

cards.front: In a STAR answer, the ‘A’ should emphasize:
cards.back: **Your specific actions and decisions** — ‘We’ stories hide your contribution — interviewers evaluate you, so make your decisions explicit.

cards.front: An SRE behavioral answer should emphasize:
cards.back: **Decisions under pressure, communication, and systemic learning** — Reliability is a team sport; the graded behaviors are judgment and coordination.

cards.front: Regions vs Availability Zones?
cards.back: Region: geographic area. AZ: isolated data center(s) within a region with independent power/network. Design rule: run across ≥2 AZs for HA; regions are for disaster recovery and data residency. The interview line: ‘one AZ is a single point of failure.’

cards.front: What is the shared-responsibility model?
cards.back: The provider secures OF the cloud (physical, hypervisor, network fabric); you secure what’s IN it (data, IAM, OS, app config). The interview trap: ‘the cloud is secure’ — no, your S3 bucket policy is your job.

cards.front: What does Docker actually give you?
cards.back: A portable, reproducible runtime: the image bundles code + dependencies + OS userland, so ‘works on my machine’ dies. Containers share the host kernel (lighter than VMs, weaker isolation) — and the interview follow-up is always about image size and layer caching.

cards.front: CapEx vs OpEx in cloud interviews?
cards.back: CapEx: buy servers upfront (fixed, depreciating). OpEx: pay per use (variable, scales with demand). Cloud’s pitch is OpEx agility — but the honest follow-up is FinOps: without governance, variable spend surprises you.

cards.front: Vendor-neutral vs vendor-specific knowledge?
cards.back: Neutral: concepts that transfer (VPCs, IAM, queues, object storage). Specific: the console clicks and service quirks. The interview line: ‘I learn the concept once, the console twice — concepts transfer, click-paths don’t.’

cards.front: How do you answer 'why not just buy servers?'
cards.back: With the honest math: steady-state 24/7 can be close on price, but the cloud buys elasticity for spiky workloads, managed undifferentiated work (backups, patching, failover), and provisioning speed. The follow-up they want: 'and without FinOps governance, variable spend surprises you.' The interview line: 'CapEx is a bet; OpEx is a meter — I choose by workload shape.'

cards.front: How do you discuss regions vs AZs for resilience?
cards.back: AZs: isolated failure domains in a region (power, network). Regions: geographic separation for disasters and compliance. The interview line: ‘AZs survive rack failures; regions survive hurricanes.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in elasticity vs scalability?
cards.back: Scalability: handling more load. Elasticity: scaling up AND down automatically with demand — the cloud’s distinctive trick. The interview line: ‘elasticity is scalability with a down arrow.’

cards.front: Leading with vendor-neutral concepts in an interview is strong because:
cards.back: **It proves transferable understanding, not memorized console paths** — Concepts survive provider changes; click-path knowledge expires with the UI.

cards.front: Cloud’s OpEx model primarily buys:
cards.back: **Agility — spend scales with demand instead of upfront provisioning** — Pay-per-use trades fixed capacity bets for variable spend — with cost governance as the required discipline.

cards.front: Containers differ from VMs in that they:
cards.back: **Share the host OS kernel instead of virtualizing hardware** — No guest kernel per container: faster startup, denser packing, but a shared kernel attack surface.

cards.front: Under shared responsibility, an open S3 bucket is:
cards.back: **The customer’s fault — data access control is in the customer’s layer** — The provider secures the service; you configure who can read your objects.

cards.front: VPC, subnets, route tables — the 60-second version?
cards.back: VPC: your isolated network. Subnets: public (route to internet gateway) vs private (no direct inbound, NAT for outbound). Route tables decide where packets go; security groups (stateful, instance-level) and NACLs (stateless, subnet-level) filter them.

cards.front: How do you design multi-AZ networking in an interview?
cards.back: VPC spanning AZs, public subnets with NAT gateways per AZ for outbound, private subnets for workloads, and no single-AZ chokepoints — cross-AZ traffic costs money, so place chatty tiers together. The interview line: ‘multi-AZ networking is redundancy you can draw and a bill you can predict.’

cards.front: What do cloud load balancers do beyond spreading traffic?
cards.back: Health checks (route only to healthy targets), TLS termination, sticky sessions when needed, and L7 routing (path/host rules). The interview line: ‘the LB is the first reliability device in the path.’

cards.front: How do you discuss DNS in cloud interviews?
cards.back: Public DNS for the world, private hosted zones for internal service discovery, TTLs controlling change propagation, and health-checked routing policies for failover. The interview line: ‘DNS is the control plane everyone forgets until it breaks.’

cards.front: NAT vs VPN vs peering?
cards.back: NAT: private resources reach the internet outbound. VPN: encrypted tunnel extending your network (site-to-site or client). Peering: private VPC-to-VPC connectivity without internet. The interview line: ‘each answers a different ‘how do these networks talk’ question.’

cards.front: Security group vs NACL — when does the difference actually bite?
cards.back: Security groups are stateful (return traffic auto-allowed) at the instance level; NACLs are stateless (both directions need rules) at the subnet level. It bites when SSH works through the security group but the NACL blocks the ephemeral-port return — connection hangs, not refused. The interview line: 'stateful forgives; stateless makes you write both directions.'

cards.front: How do you discuss VPC endpoints (PrivateLink)?
cards.back: Private connectivity to managed services without internet traversal — no NAT, no public IPs, tighter blast radius. The interview line: ‘endpoints keep cloud traffic off the internet.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in transit gateways?
cards.back: Hub-and-spoke for many VPCs: one gateway instead of N×N peering — with route-table segmentation for isolation. The interview line: ‘peering scales quadratically; transit scales linearly.’

cards.front: VPC flow logs show:
cards.back: **Allowed/rejected IP traffic metadata — who tried to reach whom** — Flow logs are the packet-level audit trail for security-group and routing diagnosis.

cards.front: VPC peering is preferred over public IPs for inter-VPC traffic because:
cards.back: **Traffic stays on the private backbone — no internet exposure** — Private routing beats public routing for both security and latency.

cards.front: A low TTL on a DNS record is used when:
cards.back: **You expect to change the target soon and need fast propagation** — Low TTL trades query volume for agility: changes propagate as fast as the TTL allows.

cards.front: Load balancer health checks matter because:
cards.back: **Traffic must avoid dead targets — the LB routes only to passing instances** — Without health checks, the balancer sprays traffic onto broken instances.

cards.front: How do you handle file uploads at scale?
cards.back: Direct-to-object-storage uploads (presigned URLs — the app server never proxies bytes), async processing (thumbnails, virus scan) via queues, CDN in front for reads. The interview line: ‘bytes never touch my app servers.’

cards.front: What do managed SQL services buy you?
cards.back: Backups, patching, failover, and read replicas handled by the provider — you keep schema design and query tuning. The interview line: ‘I outsource the undifferentiated heavy lifting, not the data model.’

cards.front: How do you discuss managed NoSQL in a cloud interview?
cards.back: By access pattern: key-value (DynamoDB-style single-digit-ms lookups), document (flexible JSON), wide-column (massive write scale). The interview line: ‘I choose the NoSQL by the query pattern, then take the managed version of that choice.’

cards.front: How do you discuss caching in a cloud interview?
cards.back: What to cache (read-heavy, slow-changing), where (CDN edge, app cache, DB query cache), invalidation strategy, and the failure story (thundering herd, stale reads). The interview line: ‘caching is a tradeoff with an invalidation plan, not a speedup.’

cards.front: How do you manage data lifecycle and tiering?
cards.back: Classify by access pattern and compliance needs: hot (frequent, fast storage), warm, cold/archive (cheap, slow retrieval). Automate transitions with lifecycle policies; the interview line: ‘every byte has a cost curve — tiering matches cost to value.’

cards.front: How do you answer 'SQL or NoSQL?' without sounding religious?
cards.back: By access pattern: relational integrity and ad-hoc queries → managed SQL; single-digit-ms key lookups → key-value; flexible documents → document store. Then the managed caveat: 'I choose the NoSQL by the query pattern, then take the managed version of that choice.' The interview line: 'the workload picks the store; I just read its requirements.'

cards.front: How do you discuss backup vs replication?
cards.back: Replication is availability (survives node loss); backup is recoverability (survives data loss and human error) — you need both. The interview line: ‘replication won’t save you from DELETE FROM.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in data residency?
cards.back: Where data lives and crosses borders: region selection, compliance constraints, and the replication topology that honors them. The interview line: ‘residency is a legal requirement wearing an architecture costume.’

cards.front: RPO and RTO define:
cards.back: **How much data loss is tolerable and how fast recovery must complete** — RPO bounds data loss (backup frequency); RTO bounds downtime (recovery speed).

cards.front: Archiving compliance data to glacier-class storage is justified because:
cards.back: **Rarely-accessed retention data shouldn’t pay hot-storage prices** — Storage cost should follow access frequency; compliance retention is the classic cold tier.

cards.front: Every caching decision must name:
cards.back: **The invalidation strategy — stale data is caching’s permanent tax** — Cache without an invalidation story is a future incident.

cards.front: Managed NoSQL’s pitch is:
cards.back: **Operational burden offloaded — scaling, patching, and failover handled** — You keep the data-model decisions; the provider keeps the cluster healthy.

cards.front: How do you explain defense in depth for cloud?
cards.back: Layers that fail independently: identity (least-privilege IAM), network (security groups, NACLs, private subnets), data (encryption at rest and in transit, KMS), and detective controls (audit logs, Config rules). The interview line: ‘no single layer is trusted; the stack is the control.’

cards.front: How do you do IAM least privilege in practice?
cards.back: Roles over users, policies scoped to specific actions on specific resources, no wildcards in production, permission boundaries and SCPs as guardrails, regular access reviews. The interview line: ‘every permission has a reason and an expiry conversation.’

cards.front: How do you secure APIs at the cloud edge?
cards.back: Authentication at the API gateway (not in each service), WAF rules for L7 attacks, throttling and quotas per key, and private APIs behind VPC endpoints for internal traffic. The interview line: ‘the edge is where auth, abuse protection, and rate limits live once, not N times.’

cards.front: How do you manage secrets in the cloud?
cards.back: Dedicated secret managers (rotation, audit, fine-grained access) — never env files in repos, never baked into images. Apps fetch at runtime with their workload role. The interview line: ‘secrets are fetched, not shipped.’

cards.front: What are cloud guardrails?
cards.back: Preventive: SCPs and permission boundaries that make bad actions impossible. Detective: Config rules and CloudTrail audit trails that catch what happened. The interview line: ‘guardrails make the safe path the easy path.’

cards.front: What's the first thing you check in an unfamiliar cloud account?
cards.back: Identity: who has what access. Users without MFA, wildcard admin policies, and ancient access keys are the fastest wins — most breaches start at identity, not at the firewall. The interview line: 'I audit the front door before the windows.'

cards.front: How do you discuss KMS envelope encryption?
cards.back: Data keys encrypt the data; master keys in KMS encrypt the data keys — rotation and audit at the master level. The interview line: ‘envelope encryption makes key rotation cheap.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in SCPs vs IAM policies?
cards.back: SCPs: guardrails on what an account CAN do (even admins). IAM: what an identity may do. The interview line: ‘SCPs set the ceiling; IAM works under it.’

cards.front: CloudTrail’s primary purpose is:
cards.back: **An audit log of who did what via the API — the forensic record** — Every API call recorded with identity and time: the basis for incident forensics and compliance.

cards.front: Baking secrets into container images is wrong because:
cards.back: **Anyone with registry access gets the secrets — images are widely shared artifacts** — Images travel through registries and caches; secrets must be injected at runtime, not build time.

cards.front: Creating the same resource twice with POST vs PUT: the key difference is:
cards.back: **PUT is idempotent — repeating it has the same effect; POST is not guaranteed to be** — Idempotency is the contract: safe retries depend on it.

cards.front: An IAM policy with Action: ‘*’ on Resource: ‘*’ is:
cards.back: **A violation of least privilege — blast radius is the whole account** — Wildcard-everything grants total control; compromise of those credentials compromises the account.

notes.title: Worked example: CloudTrail’s primary purpose is:
notes.body:
**Problem.** CloudTrail’s primary purpose is:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** An audit log of who did what via the API — the forensic record
- **Why:** Every API call recorded with identity and time: the basis for incident forensics and compliance.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Every API call recorded with identity and time: the basis for incident forensics and compliance.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

cards.front: How do you open a cloud architecture design round?
cards.back: Requirements first (users, data, compliance), then region and AZ placement with the cost and latency reasoning stated, then the reference shape (edge → compute → data), then failure modes. The interview line: ‘I draw the blast radius before I draw the boxes.’

cards.front: Walk the classic three-tier cloud architecture.
cards.back: Presentation (ALB + CDN) → application (auto-scaled compute across AZs) → data (managed DB with replicas, caches). Public subnets for the LB, private for app and data. The interview line: ‘tiers are failure and scaling boundaries, not just boxes.’

cards.front: How do you present a cloud architecture with cost honesty?
cards.back: IaC for the whole stack (reproducible, reviewable), a cost estimate with assumptions stated (requests, storage, transfer — transfer is the surprise line item), and the tradeoff: ‘here’s what drives the bill and the lever that moves it.’

cards.front: What’s an ADR, and why do architects write them?
cards.back: Architecture Decision Record: the decision, context, alternatives considered, and consequences — the ‘why’ behind the design. Paired with a failure-mode review (what breaks, how we degrade). The interview line: ‘ADRs are how architecture survives team turnover.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Requirements and constraints'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: How do you present architecture tradeoffs without rambling?
cards.back: Three beats per decision: the choice, what it costs (money, complexity, latency), and when you'd choose differently. Then stop and invite the follow-up. The interview line: 'every architecture is a list of paid prices — I show the receipts.'

cards.front: How do you present a costed architecture honestly?
cards.back: State assumptions (requests, data, transfer), name the cost drivers, and show the scaling math — ranges, not false precision. The interview line: ‘a cost estimate without assumptions is fiction.’

cards.front: What makes an ADR worth writing?
cards.back: The decision, context, alternatives considered, and consequences — the reasoning future-you will need. The interview line: ‘ADRs are the architecture’s memory.’

cards.front: A failure-mode review asks:
cards.back: **What breaks, how the system degrades, and whether that degradation is acceptable** — Designing for the unhappy path is what separates architecture from diagramming.

cards.front: Data transfer is the classic cloud cost surprise because:
cards.back: **Architectures that chat across AZs/regions pay per GB — it compounds silently** — Egress and cross-AZ transfer bill by volume; chatty designs pay continuously.

cards.front: The app tier sits in private subnets because:
cards.back: **Only the load balancer needs internet exposure — app servers stay unreachable directly** — Minimizing internet-facing surface: one controlled entry point, defense in depth behind it.

cards.front: An ‘ambiguous layout’ warning means:
cards.back: **The constraints don’t fully determine position/size — the solver is guessing** — Ambiguity = under-constrained; conflicts = over-constrained. Different problems, different fixes.

cards.front: How do you handle cloud mock rounds (architecture design, deep dives)?
cards.back: Architecture: requirements → reference design → costed, with tradeoffs narrated. Deep dive: one service’s internals (how the LB, the queue, the DB actually work) — mechanism, not marketing. The interview line: ‘I can draw it and I can explain the boxes.’

cards.front: ‘Design X on AWS’ — how do you narrate cost and tradeoffs?
cards.back: Name the managed services you’d use and why, state the cost drivers honestly (transfer, provisioned capacity), and offer the cheaper alternative with its tradeoff. The interview line: ‘I’ll show you the Cadillac and the Honda, and tell you when each wins.’

cards.front: How do behavioral rounds differ for SREs?
cards.back: They probe ownership under pressure: on-call stories, incident decisions, disagreements about risk, and learning from outages — all STAR, all blameless. The interview line: ‘SRE behavioral rounds grade how I act when the pager fires.’

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?
cards.back: Stop learning new topics; redrill weak patterns from your debrief log, run full timed mocks, fix sleep, and rehearse your story bank aloud. The taper converts knowledge into performance — cramming new material now only adds noise.

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Mock architecture-design round'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: How do you handle 'design X' when you've never built X?
cards.back: Fall back to the shapes you know: requirements first, then map X onto three-tier, queue, or event-driven patterns, stating the mapping aloud. Interviewers grade method transfer, not prior exposure. The interview line: 'I haven't built this exact system; here's how I'd reason about it from patterns I have built.'

cards.front: What does the cloud mock’s architecture round score?

cards.front: How do you discuss the OWASP Top 10 without just listing it?
cards.back: As risk categories with a current example each: injection, broken access control, crypto failures, SSRF, and so on — then pivot to YOUR experience: ‘here’s how I found one in code review and what the fix was.’ Categories frame; stories score.

cards.front: XSS types and the fix?
cards.back: Stored (persisted, served to victims), reflected (in a crafted URL), DOM-based (client-side sink). The fix: output encoding/contextual escaping, Content-Security-Policy as defense in depth, and frameworks’ auto-escaping — never innerHTML with untrusted data.

cards.front: What auth flaws do you hunt in code review?
cards.back: Broken authentication (credential stuffing without rate limits, weak session handling), broken object-level authorization (IDOR), missing function-level checks, JWT ‘none’ algorithm or missing expiry validation. The interview line: ‘I check every endpoint for ‘who can call this’ — not just the login page.’

cards.front: What’s SSRF and why is it nasty in the cloud?
cards.back: Server-Side Request Forgery: the server fetches attacker-chosen URLs — in cloud, that means the instance metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254) and credential theft. Fixes: allowlist egress, validate/sanitize URLs, block metadata IP, IMDSv2. (Deserialization: never unserialize untrusted data — it’s remote code execution.)

cards.front: What do you look for in a security code review?
cards.back: Injection sinks, auth checks on every route, crypto done right (no custom algorithms), secrets handling, error messages that don’t leak internals, and dependency versions. The interview line: ‘I review the trust boundaries first — where untrusted data enters.’

cards.front: How do you prioritize AppSec findings in an interview?
cards.back: By exploitability times impact: reachable-by-attacker and data-touching first, theoretical second. Frame each as risk with a concrete fix and an effort estimate. The interview line: ‘a finding without a fix and a severity is just a complaint.’

cards.front: How do you discuss broken access control?
cards.back: The OWASP #1: missing function-level checks, IDOR, privilege escalation — test every route as every role. The interview line: ‘the URL is not the authorization.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in security headers?
cards.back: CSP, HSTS, frame-ancestors, and cookie flags (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite) — cheap, high-leverage defenses. The interview line: ‘headers are the cheapest security you’ll ever ship.’

cards.front: Error messages that include stack traces are a finding because:
cards.back: **They leak internals (paths, versions, queries) that aid attackers** — Information disclosure sharpens every subsequent attack; production errors stay generic.

cards.front: SSRF’s cloud nightmare scenario is:
cards.back: **Hitting the instance metadata service to steal temporary credentials** — The metadata endpoint is one hop from the vulnerable server — credentials included.

cards.front: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) means:
cards.back: **Changing an object ID in a request accesses another user’s data — missing authorization check** — Authentication proves who you are; authorization must then prove you may touch this object.

cards.front: The root fix for XSS is:
cards.back: **Context-appropriate output encoding of untrusted data (+ CSP in depth)** — XSS is code/data confusion in the browser; encoding keeps untrusted data as data.

cards.front: Walk the TLS handshake at interview depth.
cards.back: ClientHello (ciphers) → ServerHello + certificate → key exchange (ECDHE for forward secrecy) → encrypted session. Validate: cert chain to a trusted root, hostname match, expiry — and pinning for high-value mobile/API clients.

cards.front: How do you talk about firewalls and segmentation?
cards.back: Defense in depth through zones: public DMZ, app tier, data tier — traffic only flows where explicitly allowed, east-west as well as north-south. The interview line: ‘segmentation turns one breach into a contained incident instead of a network-wide event.’

cards.front: What does zero trust actually require?
cards.back: ‘Never trust, always verify’: identity-based access (not network location), least privilege, device posture, continuous verification, micro-segmentation. The interview line: ‘the VPN perimeter is dead; every request authenticates and authorizes.’

cards.front: What’s DNS security in practice?
cards.back: DNSSEC for integrity (responses are signed), DoH/DoT for query privacy, monitoring for tunneling/exfiltration (long odd queries), and registrar hygiene (locks, MFA). The interview line: ‘DNS is trusted by everything and verified by almost nothing — I verify.’

cards.front: How do you discuss DDoS mitigation?
cards.back: Layers: edge absorption (CDN/anycast scrubbing), rate limiting, WAF rules for L7, and capacity headroom. Distinguish volumetric (bandwidth) from application-layer (expensive requests) — they need different defenses. The interview line: ‘you don’t outrun a botnet; you absorb and filter at the edge.’

cards.front: What does TLS actually guarantee — and what doesn't it?
cards.back: It guarantees confidentiality and integrity in transit to the authenticated endpoint — not that the endpoint is trustworthy, not that the app behind it is safe. Phishing sites have valid certs. The interview line: 'TLS secures the pipe; it says nothing about what's drinking from it.'

cards.front: How do you discuss certificate lifecycle?
cards.back: Issuance, renewal automation (ACME), expiry monitoring — expired certs are the most embarrassing outage. The interview line: ‘certs expire; automation doesn’t forget.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in network segmentation beyond VLANs?
cards.back: Microsegmentation and identity-aware policies: least-privilege east-west, not just a DMZ perimeter. The interview line: ‘the perimeter moved to the workload.’

cards.front: Wireshark showing repeated TCP retransmissions indicates:
cards.back: **Packet loss or an unresponsive peer — a network-path problem, not application logic** — Retransmits are the transport layer saying ‘my packets aren’t getting through.’

cards.front: Application-layer (L7) DDoS differs from volumetric in that it:
cards.back: **Uses expensive legitimate-looking requests — filtering needs behavioral/WAF rules, not just bandwidth** — A few thousand costly requests can hurt more than gigabits of junk; defense is semantic.

cards.front: DNS tunneling exfiltrates data by:
cards.back: **Encoding data in DNS queries to an attacker-controlled domain — DNS is rarely filtered** — DNS’s ubiquity makes it a covert channel; monitoring query patterns catches it.

cards.front: Zero trust’s core shift is:
cards.back: **Access decisions from identity and context, not network location** — Being inside the network grants nothing; every request proves who/what it is.

notes.title: Worked example: Wireshark showing repeated TCP retransmissions indicates:
notes.body:
**Problem.** Wireshark showing repeated TCP retransmissions indicates:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Packet loss or an unresponsive peer — a network-path problem, not application logic
- **Why:** Retransmits are the transport layer saying ‘my packets aren’t getting through.’

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Retransmits are the transport layer saying ‘my packets aren’t getting through.’* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.
