cards.front: Symmetric vs asymmetric crypto — the interview version?
cards.back: Symmetric (AES): one shared key, fast — for bulk data. Asymmetric (RSA/ECDH): key pairs, slow — for key exchange and signatures. Hybrid in practice: asymmetric establishes, symmetric encrypts. The interview line: ‘asymmetric for trust, symmetric for speed.’

cards.front: How do you store passwords — the security interview version?
cards.back: Argon2id (or bcrypt) with unique per-user salts and a tuned work factor; pepper via KMS/HSM as defense in depth. Never MD5/SHA-256 alone (too fast — GPUs crack them), never reversible encryption.

cards.front: What’s ‘TLS in practice’ beyond the handshake?
cards.back: Version and cipher hygiene (TLS 1.2+, strong suites), cert lifecycle (automation via ACME, expiry monitoring), HSTS, and pinning for high-value clients. The interview line: ‘handshake knowledge gets you hired; lifecycle hygiene keeps you employed.’

cards.front: What does real key management look like?
cards.back: Keys in a KMS/HSM, never in code or repos; envelope encryption; rotation on a schedule and on incident; separate keys per environment/data class; audit every use. The interview line: ‘if I can see the key in the repo, we’ve already lost.’

cards.front: What does ‘randomness done right’ mean?
cards.back: Cryptographic randomness (CSPRNG: /dev/urandom, secrets module) for keys, tokens, and nonces — never Math.random() or seeded PRNGs for security purposes. The interview line: ‘predictable randomness is no randomness.’

cards.front: How do you answer 'should we encrypt it twice for safety'?
cards.back: With the threat model: double encryption adds complexity and key-management burden for marginal gain — the risk is almost never the cipher, it's the keys, the randomness, and the implementation. Fix the key management first. The interview line: 'I don't armor the vault door while the keys hang on a hook beside it.'

cards.front: How do you discuss hashing vs encryption for passwords?
cards.back: Hashing is one-way (verification without recovery); encryption is reversible (a breached key exposes all). The interview line: ‘passwords are verified, never decrypted.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in forward secrecy?
cards.back: Ephemeral key exchange (ECDHE) so a future key compromise can’t decrypt past traffic. The interview line: ‘forward secrecy bounds the blast radius of a stolen key.’

cards.front: Custom crypto is dangerous because:
cards.back: **Subtle flaws survive testing and review — even experts get it wrong; use vetted primitives** — Cryptographic failures are silent until exploited; peer-reviewed primitives are the only sane choice.

cards.front: Math.random() is unfit for security tokens because:
cards.back: **It’s a predictable PRNG — outputs can be reconstructed by attackers** — Non-cryptographic PRNGs have observable state; CSPRNGs are designed to resist prediction.

cards.front: Key rotation limits damage because:
cards.back: **A leaked key has a bounded useful lifetime** — Rotation shrinks the window where a compromised key is valuable.

cards.front: Certificate expiry monitoring matters because:
cards.back: **Expired certs are a top-5 outage cause — entirely preventable with automation** — Letting certs expire is an unforced outage; ACME + monitoring ends it.

cards.front: How do you use MITRE ATT&CK in an interview?
cards.back: As a shared map of adversary behavior: tactics (why — initial access, persistence, exfiltration) → techniques (how). Detection engineering maps log sources to techniques and writes detections per technique — coverage measured against the matrix, not vibes.

cards.front: What makes detection engineering real?
cards.back: Detections mapped to ATT&CK techniques, built on log sources you’ve verified produce the needed telemetry, tuned for signal (precision/recall on alerts), and tested with simulated adversary activity. The interview line: ‘a detection without a tested log source is a hope.’

cards.front: Walk the incident response phases.
cards.back: Preparation → Detection & Analysis → Containment → Eradication → Recovery → Lessons Learned (NIST 800-61). The interview emphasis: contain before you eradicate (don’t tip off the adversary / destroy evidence), and lessons-learned feeds back into preparation.

cards.front: How do you tell a breach story in an interview?
cards.back: Blameless framing, the timeline as you understood it then, what the investigation actually showed, the action items with owners — and what you personally changed afterward. The interview line: ‘I talk about what the incident taught the system, not who failed.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'ATT&CK as a map'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: How do you measure detection coverage without vibes?
cards.back: Against the ATT&CK matrix: techniques mapped to log sources mapped to tested detections — the uncovered techniques are the gaps, named explicitly. Coverage is a spreadsheet, not a feeling. The interview line: 'show me the matrix with the holes highlighted.'

cards.front: How do you discuss false positives in detection?
cards.back: Tune with baselines, tier by fidelity, and measure precision — alert fatigue kills response. The interview line: ‘a detection nobody trusts is a decoration.’

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in log source verification?
cards.back: Proving the telemetry exists before writing the rule: the event, the fields, the volume. The interview line: ‘detections are only as real as their log sources.’

cards.front: A breach story should emphasize:
cards.back: **Timeline, evidence-driven findings, and systemic fixes with owners** — Interviewers score learning and systems thinking — blame and heroics score nothing.

cards.front: Containment comes before eradication because:
cards.back: **You stop the bleeding and preserve evidence before removing the threat** — Eradicating first can destroy forensic evidence and alert the adversary mid-investigation.

cards.front: A detection rule needs tuning because:
cards.back: **Untuned rules alert on benign activity — alert fatigue kills the SOC’s trust** — Precision matters as much as recall: a noisy rule gets ignored, then the real alert dies in the noise.

cards.front: ATT&CK’s tactics vs techniques distinction is:
cards.back: **Tactics are adversary goals; techniques are how they achieve them** — The hierarchy lets defenders map ‘what could happen’ to ‘what we’d see’ systematically.

cards.front: How do you run a STRIDE threat model quickly?
cards.back: Per component/data flow, ask: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. Enumerate threats, rank by risk, assign mitigations with owners. The interview line: ‘threat modeling is structured pessimism with a spreadsheet.’

cards.front: How do you review a sample architecture in an interview?
cards.back: Systematically: trust boundaries, data flows, failure modes, scaling story, cost drivers — then findings risk-ranked with concrete fixes. The interview line: ‘I review like an attacker and report like a consultant.’

cards.front: How do you design authentication for a new service?
cards.back: Threat-model first (what are we protecting from whom), then: phishing-resistant MFA where it matters, short-lived tokens, secure session handling, rate-limited login, and secrets in a manager — never in config. The interview line: ‘auth design starts from the threat model, not the library.’

cards.front: How do you present security findings like a consultant?
cards.back: Risk-ranked, evidence-backed, and actionable: finding → impact in business terms → likelihood → concrete remediation with effort estimate. Lead with the criticals, never with a 200-item undifferentiated list.

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Threat modeling: STRIDE lite'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: How do you threat-model when you only have 10 minutes?
cards.back: STRIDE-lite on the highest-risk data flow only: enumerate fast, rank by obvious impact, mitigate the top 3 with owners. A partial model of the riskiest flow beats a complete model of nothing. The interview line: 'threat modeling is triage with a threat vocabulary.'

cards.front: How do you discuss trust boundaries in a design review?
cards.back: Every crossing is an attack surface: validate at the boundary, never trust the caller. The interview line: ‘the boundary is where the threat model lives.’

cards.front: What makes a security finding actionable?
cards.back: Risk-ranked, evidence-backed, with a concrete fix and effort estimate — written for the builder, not the auditor. The interview line: ‘findings ship when the fix is obvious.’

cards.front: A security review should lead with:
cards.back: **Risk-ranked criticals with business impact and concrete fixes** — Decision-makers need prioritization: what burns first, what it costs, how to fix it.

cards.front: Short-lived access tokens limit damage because:
cards.back: **A stolen token is useful only briefly — the exposure window shrinks** — Token lifetime bounds the value of theft; refresh tokens (rotated, bound) handle continuity.

cards.front: Leading the review with trust boundaries is strong because:
cards.back: **Security architecture is about where untrusted data crosses — boundaries frame everything** — Every finding lives at a boundary; mapping them first organizes the review.

cards.front: In STRIDE, ‘Repudiation’ threats are about:
cards.back: **An attacker denying their actions — fixed with non-repudiation (audit logs, signatures)** — Without tamper-evident logs, attackers can plausibly deny what they did.

notes.body: Preparation only — this course confers no certificate, and a classroom review is not a professional security assessment. Real reviews involve stakeholder negotiation, incomplete information, and liability that no exercise carries; the module teaches the review structure and the consultant's reporting discipline. notes.title: Worked example: A security review should lead with:
notes.body:
**Problem.** A security review should lead with:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Risk-ranked criticals with business impact and concrete fixes
- **Why:** Decision-makers need prioritization: what burns first, what it costs, how to fix it.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Decision-makers need prioritization: what burns first, what it costs, how to fix it.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

cards.front: How do you handle security mock rounds?
cards.back: Secure design: threat-model aloud (STRIDE-lite), name mitigations per threat. Attacker mindset: think in exploit primitives from the code/architecture. Incident response: contain before eradicate, preserve evidence. The interview line: ‘I show the thinking, not just the answer.’

cards.front: How do you tell a breach story in an interview?
cards.back: Blameless framing, the timeline as you understood it then, what the investigation actually showed, the action items with owners — and what you personally changed afterward. The interview line: ‘I talk about what the incident taught the system, not who failed.’

cards.front: What goes in a security engineer’s portfolio?
cards.back: Writeups that show method: a threat model, a code-review finding with the fix, a detection rule with its tuning rationale, a post-incident review — sanitized, of course. The interview line: ‘I show how I think, not just what I found.’

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?
cards.back: Stop learning new topics; redrill weak patterns from your debrief log, run full timed mocks, fix sleep, and rehearse your story bank aloud. The taper converts knowledge into performance — cramming new material now only adds noise.

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Mock secure-design round'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

cards.front: How do you answer 'have you ever been breached?' honestly?
cards.back: With the blameless story structure: what happened, the timeline as you understood it then, what the investigation actually showed, the systemic fixes with owners — and what you personally changed afterward. Never name others' failures; talk about what the incident taught the system. The interview line: 'I talk about what the incident taught the system, not who failed.'

cards.front: How do you prep the attacker-mindset round?
cards.back: Think in abuse cases: how would you break this feature? Then flip to mitigations. The interview line: ‘attack first, defend second — in that order.’

cards.front: What does the secure-design mock score?
cards.back: Threat modeling aloud, mitigations per threat, and tradeoff honesty — the STRIDE-lite walkthrough. The interview line: ‘the model is the message.’

cards.front: The taper period’s rule is:
cards.back: **No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest** — Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

cards.front: A portfolio writeup’s most valuable element is:
cards.back: **The reasoning: how you found it, why it matters, how you’d fix and verify it** — Method transfers across jobs; any single finding doesn’t.

cards.front: A breach story should emphasize:
cards.back: **Timeline, evidence-driven findings, and systemic fixes with owners** — Interviewers score learning and systems thinking — blame and heroics score nothing.

cards.front: Thinking aloud in security rounds is graded because:
cards.back: **Security judgment is the product — the reasoning is what’s being evaluated** — Two candidates can name the same control; the reasoning separates them.

cards.front: When do you reach for two pointers?
cards.back: Ordered data and pair-finding: opposite ends for sorted two-sum or container-with-most-water; same-direction fast/slow pointers for cycle detection or in-place dedup — O(n) time, O(1) space. Name which variant and why.

cards.front: How do you speed-rep DSA fundamentals?
cards.back: Pattern batches under time: trees/graphs/heaps one session (traversals, BFS/DFS, top-k), DP basics the next (1D ladder, knapsack shapes) — always stating complexity aloud. The interview line: ‘speed reps build the reflex; the debrief builds the skill.’

cards.front: How do you handle the 30-minute coding bar?
cards.back: Budget aloud: 5 min clarify + plan, 20 min code, 5 min test. Start with brute force stated and its complexity (it buys time and shows honesty), then optimize the bottleneck. A working brute force beats a half-written optimal.

cards.front: Why say complexity out loud?
cards.back: Because the interviewer can’t grade silent thought: stating ‘this is O(n) time, O(1) space because…’ at each step turns reasoning into evidence. It’s also your early-warning system — saying it forces you to check it.

cards.front: How do you review wrong answers productively?
cards.back: Classify the miss: wrong pattern, bug in implementation, complexity fumble, or time management — then redrill the class, not just the problem. The interview line: ‘I fix the category, not the instance.’

cards.front: How do you choose between BFS and DFS in an interview?
cards.back: BFS for shortest path in unweighted graphs and level-order needs; DFS for connectivity, cycles, topological shapes, and when recursion depth is safe. State the choice and its complexity before coding — the choice is part of the graded reasoning. The interview line: 'BFS for distance, DFS for structure.'

cards.front: What does a DSA speed-rep session look like?
cards.back: Pattern batches under time: one pattern family per session, timed solves, miss-category logging. The interview line: ‘reps build pattern recognition; the timer builds the interview.’

cards.front: How do you review a timed solve that was correct but slow?
cards.back: Find the hesitation point: recognition, implementation, or testing — then drill that phase. The interview line: ‘slow correct beats fast wrong, but the clock still counts.’

cards.front: Redrilling the miss category (not just the problem) works because:
cards.back: **Interviews test categories under new disguises — the instance never repeats** — The next problem will wear a different costume; the category is what transfers.

cards.front: Stating complexity aloud during coding:
cards.back: **Makes your reasoning gradable and forces self-checks** — Verbalized reasoning is scorable reasoning — and it catches your own mistakes mid-stream.

cards.front: Stating the brute force first is strong because:
cards.back: **It shows honest complexity reasoning and gives a working fallback while you optimize** — A correct slow solution on the board beats a blank editor; optimization then has a baseline.

cards.front: Speed reps should always include stating complexity aloud because:
cards.back: **The interview grades the analysis as well as the code — rehearse both together** — Rehearsing code without narration trains half the interview.

cards.front: How do you open a system design round?
cards.back: Requirements before architecture: restate functional requirements (what the system does), then non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency). Scoping first proves you design the right system — candidates who draw boxes before asking get failed.

cards.front: How do you do API + data-model design in a system-design rep?
cards.back: Resources and verbs first, then the storage that serves the access patterns — the two designed together, since API shape constrains queries and data shape constrains the API. The interview line: ‘the API and the model are one decision, not two.’

cards.front: How do you talk about scaling levers?
cards.back: The three moves: shard the data (split the load), cache the hot paths (skip the work), queue the spikes (defer the work). The interview line: ‘scaling is choosing which of the three each bottleneck needs.’

cards.front: How do you prep the classic designs (shortener, feed, chat)?
cards.back: One page each: requirements, estimation, the 2–3 key decisions, the scaling story. The classics are classics because they each teach one lesson — shortener: IDs and caching; feed: fan-out; chat: real-time. The interview line: ‘I learn the lesson, not the diagram.’

cards.front: How do you do bottleneck analysis in a design round?
cards.back: Follow the request path and ask ‘what breaks first as load grows 10x?’ at each hop — then apply the right lever (shard/cache/queue) to that hop. The interview line: ‘bottlenecks are found by walking the path, not by guessing.’

cards.front: How do you handle 'it depends' in a design round?
cards.back: 'It depends' is only a good answer when you then explain what it depends on: the workload's read/write ratio, consistency needs, and scale decide between the options — so name the deciding factors and pick for the stated case. The interview line: 'it depends on three things; here's how each would change my answer.'

cards.front: How do you prep the classic designs efficiently?
cards.back: One page each: requirements, estimation, the 2–3 key decisions, the scaling story — the classics are patterns, not scripts. The interview line: ‘prep the decisions, not the diagrams.’

cards.front: What does bottleneck analysis sound like aloud?
cards.back: ‘At 10x, the database writes saturate first — so I’d shard by user_id and cache the hot reads.’ The interview line: ‘name the first thing that breaks.’

cards.front: Labeling arrows with what flows matters because:
cards.back: **Unlabeled arrows hide the data story — the labels are where the design lives** — Architecture is data in motion; unlabeled arrows are just boxes.

cards.front: Asking ‘what breaks first at 10x’ is the right question because:
cards.back: **It forces ordered thinking about limits instead of vague ‘it scales’ claims** — Scaling claims need a named first failure; otherwise they’re wishes.

cards.front: Learning the lesson (not the diagram) matters because:
cards.back: **Interviewers vary the problem — the transferable insight is what repeats** — The next question won’t be the shortener; the ID-generation insight will recur.

cards.front: Queues handle spikes while caches handle hot data because:
cards.back: **Queues defer work in time; caches skip work entirely — different bottlenecks, different tools** — Time-shifting vs work-avoidance: match the lever to the bottleneck’s nature.

cards.front: What’s the STAR structure, and why does it work for behavioral rounds?
cards.back: Situation (2 sentences of context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what YOU did — the bulk), Result (measurable outcome + lesson). It works because interviewers score evidence of behavior, and STAR forces a complete evidence unit.

cards.front: How do you cover conflict, failure, and leadership stories?
cards.back: One banked STAR story each: conflict (disagreement handled professionally), failure (owned, with the fix), leadership (influence without authority counts). The interview line: ‘I bank all three before the loop — the questions are predictable.’

cards.front: How do you answer ‘Why this company?’ convincingly?
cards.back: Specific, researched, and tied to you: their product/technical challenges, something you learned from an employee/blog/post, and how your background maps to their problems. Generic flattery fails; specifics signal genuine interest.

cards.front: What questions should you ask the interviewer?
cards.back: Ones that reveal the job’s reality: ‘what does success look like in 6 months?’, ‘what’s the hardest technical problem the team faces?’, ‘how are on-call and incidents handled?’, ‘why is this role open?’ Never ask what the website answers.

cards.front: Why practice behavioral answers aloud — and record them?
cards.back: Aloud reveals pacing, filler, and rambling that silent rehearsal hides; recording lets you review like an interviewer. The interview line: ‘my first recording is always 40% too long — that’s what the practice is for.’

cards.front: How do you keep a STAR story under 2 minutes?
cards.back: Two sentences of situation, one of task, the bulk on your actions — and the result in one sentence plus the lesson. Everything else is cut in rehearsal, which is why you record: the timer is the editor. The interview line: 'my first recording is always 40% too long — that's what the practice is for.'

cards.front: How do you handle the weakness question?
cards.back: A real, non-fatal weakness plus the system you built to manage it — growth with evidence. The interview line: ‘the weakness is the setup; the system is the answer.’

cards.front: How do you prep stories for SRE/DevOps behavioral rounds?
cards.back: On-call and incident stories: the page, the decision, the blameless lesson — ownership under pressure. The interview line: ‘the pager stories are the portfolio.’

cards.front: Recording yourself works because:
cards.back: **You hear what the interviewer hears — pacing and filler invisible from inside** — Self-perception lies about delivery; the recording doesn’t.

cards.front: The strongest interviewer question reveals:
cards.back: **The role’s reality: success criteria, hard problems, team health** — You’re interviewing them too: these answers predict your actual day-to-day.

cards.front: ‘Why this company?’ fails when the answer:
cards.back: **Could apply to any company — no specifics about them** — Interchangeable answers reveal no research; specifics prove interest.

cards.front: Banking all three story types before the loop works because:
cards.back: **Behavioral questions are predictable — preparation converts them to free points** — The question set barely varies; rehearsed stories answer them all.

cards.front: How do you handle a domain question you can’t answer?

cards.front: What's the tradeoff question you should answer before the interviewer asks it?

notes.title: Worked example: The teach-back test works because:
notes.body:
**Problem.** The teach-back test works because:

**Step 1 — Answer from first principles.** Cover the choices and commit to an answer using only the concept, not pattern-matching. Say your reasoning out loud — in interviews and in real work, the reasoning is what gets graded.

**Step 2 — Reveal and verify.**
- **Correct answer:** Producing a clear explanation exposes gaps that recognition hides
- **Why:** Recognition ≠ recall ≠ teaching; each level demands deeper organization of knowledge.

**Step 3 — Lock in the principle.** Compress the explanation into one reusable rule: *Recognition ≠ recall ≠ teaching; each level demands deeper organization of knowledge.* Write it on a card. If you cannot state the rule without the item in front of you, you memorized the item instead of the idea.

**Step 4 — Teach it back.** Explain this item to an imaginary junior in three sentences: what was asked, what the right move was, and the one mistake to avoid. Teaching is the retention test — if the explanation wobbles, re-study before moving on.

cards.front: How do you simulate a full interview loop?
cards.back: Four timed rounds back-to-back (coding, design, domain deep-dive, behavioral) with a partner playing interviewer, scored against a rubric, then a weakness-targeting week on the lowest scores. The point: stamina and context-switching are skills you train.

cards.front: How do you warm up on loop day morning?
cards.back: One easy problem you have solved before (confidence, not learning), your story bank skimmed aloud once, and logistics handled the night before. No new topics — the morning is about activation, not acquisition. The interview line: ‘loop day is a performance; the rehearsal ended last night.’

cards.front: How do you score yourself against an interview rubric?
cards.back: Fixed axes per round type: correctness, complexity analysis, communication, time management, tradeoffs named. Score honestly after every mock; the rubric turns feelings into data. The interview line: ‘I grade myself the way they’ll grade me.’

cards.front: What’s a weakness-targeting week?
cards.back: One week between full-loop simulation and the real loop, spent only on the lowest rubric scores: targeted drills, one more mock per weak area, then rest. The interview line: ‘the week has one job — raise the floor.’

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?
cards.back: Stop learning new topics; redrill weak patterns from your debrief log, run full timed mocks, fix sleep, and rehearse your story bank aloud. The taper converts knowledge into performance — cramming new material now only adds noise.

cards.front: How do you reset between rounds on loop day?
cards.back: Fifteen minutes, same ritual: water, notes closed, one breath — the last round's mistakes don't get a vote in this one. Context-switching is a trained skill, and the reset is the training. The interview line: 'each round starts clean; I carry the rubric, not the regret.'

cards.front: How do you review a full-loop simulation?
cards.back: Score each round against its rubric, find the lowest axis, and spend the week there — the loop is only as strong as its weakest round. The interview line: ‘the simulation finds the leak; the week fixes it.’

cards.front: What goes on the loop-day packing list?
cards.back: Logistics confirmed, story bank skimmed, weak rounds redrilled, sleep protected — the 48 hours are choreography. The interview line: ‘loop day is won the week before.’

cards.front: The highest-value activity right after a mock is:
cards.back: **A written debrief naming what leaked, plus a redrill plan** — Improvement comes from the feedback loop: name the leak, target the redrill, verify next time.

cards.front: The taper period’s rule is:
cards.back: **No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest** — Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

cards.front: Targeting the floor (not the ceiling) is right because:
cards.back: **Offers are lost on weak rounds, not won on strong ones — the minimum decides** — Interview loops grade the weakest link; raising it raises the whole loop.

cards.front: Rubric scoring beats gut feeling because:
cards.back: **It makes weaknesses comparable across mocks — triage needs data** — You can’t triage what you haven’t measured.

scriptLabs.title: Error-budget calculator
scriptLabs.brief: Turn SLO math into code: given total requests, failed requests, and an SLO, compute the percentage of the error budget consumed. The arithmetic behind every burn-rate conversation.
scriptLabs.starter:
def budget_consumed(total_requests, failed_requests, slo):
    """Return the % of the error budget consumed (0-100+, may exceed 100).

    slo: e.g. 0.999 for a 99.9% SLO.
    """
    # TODO: allowed failures = total * (1 - slo); consumed % = failed / allowed * 100.
    pass
scriptLabs.hint: Budget = total × (1 − SLO); consumed % = failed ÷ allowed × 100. Guard the zero-allowed edge case.
scriptLabs.solution:
def budget_consumed(total_requests, failed_requests, slo):
    allowed = total_requests * (1 - slo)
    if allowed <= 0:
        return 100.0 if failed_requests > 0 else 0.0
    return (failed_requests / allowed) * 100

# Example: 1M requests, 500 failed, 99.9% SLO -> 50% of budget consumed.
print(budget_consumed(1_000_000, 500, 0.999))

scriptLabs.title: Production-ready Deployment manifest
scriptLabs.brief: Write a Kubernetes Deployment you’d defend in an interview: replicas, probes, resource requests/limits, and labels. The manifest is the artifact; the narration is the score.
scriptLabs.starter:
# TODO: complete this Deployment for a web API named 'api' (image api:1.4.2).
# Requirements: 3 replicas, readiness + liveness probes on /healthz,
# CPU/memory requests AND limits, app=api labels.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
scriptLabs.hint: Probes need httpGet on /healthz with initialDelaySeconds; resources need both requests and limits; matchLabels must equal the pod template labels.
scriptLabs.solution:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
  labels:
    app: api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: api:1.4.2
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "250m"
            memory: "256Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "1000m"
            memory: "512Mi"

scriptLabs.brief: Write the fast-burn Prometheus alert you’d actually ship: budget-consumption ratio over two windows, a for-duration, and a severity. Symptom-based alerting, as the module teaches.
scriptLabs.starter:
# TODO: alert when the service burns its 99.9% SLO error budget too fast.
# Metrics: http_requests_total, http_requests_failed_total (counter, label-free).
# Requirements: burn-rate expression, 'for' duration, severity label, summary annotation.
groups:
- name: slo-burn
  rules:
scriptLabs.hint: Burn rate = failed-rate / (total-rate × budget-ratio). For 99.9%, the budget ratio is 0.001; alert when the ratio exceeds ~14x over both a 1h and a 5m window.
scriptLabs.solution:
groups:
- name: slo-burn
  rules:
  - alert: HighErrorBudgetBurn
    expr: |
      (
        sum(rate(http_requests_failed_total[1h]))
        /
        sum(rate(http_requests_total[1h]))
      ) > 0.001 * 14.4
      and
      (
        sum(rate(http_requests_failed_total[5m]))
        /
        sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))
      ) > 0.001 * 14.4
    for: 15m
    labels:
      severity: critical
    annotations:
      summary: "Error budget burning 14x faster than the 99.9% SLO allows"

scriptLabs.title: Triage runbook: pods CrashLooping
scriptLabs.brief: Write the ordered triage script you’d narrate in a live troubleshooting round: from symptom to cause in kubectl commands. Hypothesis → test → observe, said out loud.
scriptLabs.starter:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Triage: pods for deployment 'api' are CrashLooping.
# TODO: ordered commands — status, events, logs, resources, recent changes.
set -euo pipefail
NS=prod
scriptLabs.hint: Order: what’s happening (get/describe) → why it dies (logs of the previous container) → resource pressure (top) → what changed (rollout history).
scriptLabs.solution:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Triage: 'api' pods CrashLooping in prod.
set -euo pipefail
NS=prod

echo "== 1. What is happening?"
kubectl get pods -n "$NS" -l app=api
kubectl describe deployment api -n "$NS" | tail -20

echo "== 2. Why did the container die? (previous container logs)"
kubectl logs -n "$NS" -l app=api --previous --tail=100 || true

echo "== 3. Resource pressure?"
kubectl top pods -n "$NS" -l app=api || true

echo "== 4. What changed recently?"
kubectl rollout history deployment/api -n "$NS"

echo "== 5. Events tell the story"
kubectl get events -n "$NS" --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20

drills.title: SLIs, SLOs, and Error Budgets
drills.prompt: When the error budget is exhausted, the correct policy is:
choices: Freeze or slow risky releases until the budget recovers
drills.explain: The budget is the agreed tradeoff dial: spending it all means reliability work comes first.

drills.title: CI/CD Systems
choices: Releasing to a small subset first and promoting based on observed metrics
drills.explain: Progressive exposure with metric gates: problems hit 1% before 100%.

drills.title: Core Cloud Concepts
drills.prompt: Leading with vendor-neutral concepts in an interview is strong because:
choices: It proves transferable understanding, not memorized console paths
drills.explain: Concepts survive provider changes; click-path knowledge expires with the UI.

drills.title: Application Security Fundamentals
choices: Hitting the instance metadata service to steal temporary credentials
drills.explain: The metadata endpoint is one hop from the vulnerable server — credentials included.

drills.title: DSA Speed Reps
drills.prompt: Redrilling the miss category (not just the problem) works because:
choices: Interviews test categories under new disguises — the instance never repeats
drills.explain: The next problem will wear a different costume; the category is what transfers.

drills.title: Budget math
drills.explain: 0.01% of 43,200 min ≈ 4.3 min. Four nines is brutal — that's the point of the arithmetic.

drills.title: First mitigation
drills.prompt: A deploy 10 minutes ago correlates with error spike. Fastest mitigation?
choices: Debug the new code in production
Roll back to the previous version, then investigate
drills.explain: Rollback restores service in minutes; root-causing can happen safely afterward. Mitigate first, diagnose second.

drills.title: Alert design
drills.prompt: Best alert for a user-facing SLO?
choices: Burn-rate-based multi-window alert on the SLI
drills.explain: Alert on the user-impacting SLI's burn rate, not on infrastructure symptoms. Multi-window avoids flapping.

drills.title: IaC interview
drills.prompt: Asked 'how do you handle Terraform state in a team?', the key points are:
choices: Remote backend with locking, separate state per environment, no secrets in state committed anywhere
drills.explain: Remote + locked + per-env state; secrets via Vault/cloud managers, never in committed state.

drills.title: Security interview
drills.prompt: 'How would you secure a CI/CD pipeline?' Lead with:
choices: OIDC short-lived credentials (no stored secrets), signed artifacts, SAST/DAST gates, least-privilege runners, audit logs
drills.explain: Pipeline security = identity (OIDC), supply chain (signing, gates), least privilege, auditability.

scenarios.title: Incident command: sev-1 checkout outage
scenarios.context: 02:14. Pager: checkout error rate 40% and climbing. You’re the on-call SRE and incident commander.

steps.prompt: First action in the opening minutes?

options.text: Declare the incident, assume IC, open the bridge and the #incident channel
options.why: Command before debugging: declaring focuses the response, the bridge gathers experts, and the IC coordinates instead of keyboard-diving.

options.text: SSH in and start debugging the checkout service alone
options.why: Solo debugging abandons command — nobody coordinates, comms go silent, and parallel work collides.

options.text: Page the entire engineering org immediately
options.why: Paging everyone is noise; page the service owners and scale only if the blast radius demands it.

options.text: Wait 10 minutes to see if it recovers on its own
options.why: 40% errors and climbing is user harm now; waiting converts an incident into a longer incident.

steps.prompt: Five minutes in, no mitigation yet. What do you communicate?

options.text: Post impact-first updates to #incident every ~15 minutes: who’s affected, what we’re doing, when the next update lands
options.why: Cadenced, impact-first comms prevent the second outage (confusion); ‘no update’ is itself an update.

options.text: Stay silent until there’s a fix to announce
options.why: Silence during an outage breeds rumors and duplicate escalations — comms is part of the response.

options.text: Post raw stack traces and theories as they occur
options.why: Unfiltered debugging noise confuses stakeholders; the comms role translates signal for the audience.

options.text: Email the CEO directly with early speculation
options.why: Escalation without facts creates pressure without progress; comms goes through the incident channel.

steps.prompt: You suspect the 02:00 deploy. Mitigation vs root cause — what now?

options.text: Roll back the deploy first (mitigate), investigate the root cause after traffic recovers
options.why: Mitigate first, understand second: every minute of 40% errors is user harm, and the rollback is the fastest hypothesis test.

options.text: Find the exact root cause before touching anything
options.why: Diagnosis-before-mitigation maximizes outage duration; the incident lifecycle puts mitigation first.

options.text: Scale up the checkout pods — more capacity fixes everything
options.why: Scaling a broken deploy multiplies the brokenness; capacity treats a symptom you haven’t diagnosed.

options.text: Restart all pods simultaneously
options.why: A full restart is a full outage during the restart — and it destroys the evidence you need.

steps.prompt: The incident is resolved. What makes the postmortem useful?

options.text: Blameless timeline, plural root causes, and action items with owners and dates
options.why: Blamelessness gets honest data; owned action items are the postmortem’s actual product — the document is just the vehicle.

options.text: A detailed account of who made the bad deploy
options.why: Blame produces cover stories in future incidents; systems and process are the fixable units.

options.text: A brief ‘all good now’ note to close the ticket
options.why: No learning, no action items — the same incident will recur on schedule.

options.text: Only the timeline, no action items
options.why: A timeline without action items is a history lesson; prevention requires owned follow-through.

scenarios.title: Design round: deployment pipeline
scenarios.context: ‘Design the CI/CD pipeline for our user-facing API.’ The interviewer wants decisions, not a tool list.

steps.prompt: Deployment strategy for the user-facing API?

options.text: Canary: small % first, promote on error-rate/latency gates, automated rollback
options.why: Progressive exposure with metric gates bounds blast radius — the right default for user-facing services.

options.text: Big-bang deploy to all instances at once — fastest
options.why: Fastest to deploy, fastest to outage: 100% of users meet every bad release simultaneously.

options.text: Manual SCP of binaries to each server
options.why: Unauditable, unrepeatable, unrollbackable — the opposite of a pipeline.

options.text: Deploy on Fridays to get it over with
options.why: Timing theater instead of safety engineering; the strategy should make any day safe.

options.text: In CI, blocking merge on critical findings — shift-left
options.why: Vulnerabilities found at commit time are cheapest to fix; blocking the merge makes the gate mechanical.

options.text: After deploy, scanned in production
options.why: Scanning prod finds vulnerabilities you’ve already shipped to attackers.

options.text: Once a year during the audit
options.why: Annual scanning leaves 364 days of unexamined changes — security theater.

options.text: Nowhere — developers are trusted
options.why: Trust isn’t a control; even excellent developers ship vulnerable dependencies unknowingly.

steps.prompt: The interviewer asks: ‘how do you roll back?’

options.text: One command redeploys the previous immutable artifact; DB migrations are backward-compatible (expand-contract)
options.why: Rollback is only real if it’s rehearsed, one command, and the data layer tolerates the old code.

options.text: ‘We’d fix forward — rollbacks are for the weak’
options.why: Fix-forward during an active outage gambles user impact on debugging speed.

options.text: Restore from last night’s backup
options.why: Backup restore loses all data since the backup and takes far longer than an artifact rollback.

options.text: We’ve never needed to roll back
options.why: ‘Never needed’ usually means ‘never tested’ — an untested rollback plan is a hope.

scenarios.title: Behavioral: ‘Tell me about an outage you handled’
scenarios.context: The SRE behavioral round. They want the war story — told like an SRE.

options.text: One with real user impact where your decisions mattered — stakes, your calls, the outcome
options.why: Impact + your decisions = gradable evidence of judgment under pressure.

options.text: The funniest outage, regardless of your role in it
options.why: Entertainment isn’t evidence; if you were a bystander, there’s nothing to score.

options.text: A story where everything went perfectly
options.why: Frictionless stories reveal nothing about how you handle pressure or ambiguity.

options.text: Someone else’s outage you heard about
options.why: Secondhand stories can’t demonstrate your behavior — interviewers score you, not your anecdotes.

steps.prompt: You made a wrong call mid-incident (restarted the wrong tier). How do you tell it?

options.text: Name it plainly: what you did, what it cost, what you changed in the runbook after
options.why: Owning mistakes with a systemic fix is the blameless-culture signal SRE teams hire for.

options.text: Leave it out — the story is cleaner without it
options.why: Sanitized stories read as fiction; the wrong turn is where the learning — and the score — lives.

options.text: Blame the misleading dashboard
options.why: Blame, even of a tool, fails the ownership test; the fix belongs to the system, including you.

options.text: Say you’d do everything the same again
options.why: No-learning answers signal no growth — the opposite of what the question probes.

steps.prompt: How do you close the story?

options.text: The lesson as a changed practice: ‘now our runbook has X, and it caught Y last month’
options.why: A lesson with evidence it stuck turns a story into proof of growth.

options.text: ‘And that’s why I’m great under pressure’
options.why: Self-praise conclusions sound hollow; let the evidence make the claim.

options.text: Trail off after the resolution
options.why: No landing wastes the story’s arc — the lesson is the point.

options.text: Ask if they’ve had similar outages
options.why: Deflecting at the close surrenders the final impression; land your lesson first.

mockTasks.q: Containers differ from VMs in that they:
choices: Share the host OS kernel instead of virtualizing hardware
mockTasks.explain: No guest kernel per container: faster startup, denser packing, but a shared kernel attack surface.

choices: Changing an object ID in a request accesses another user’s data — missing authorization check
mockTasks.explain: Authentication proves who you are; authorization must then prove you may touch this object.

mockTasks.q: Stating the brute force first is strong because:
choices: It shows honest complexity reasoning and gives a working fallback while you optimize
mockTasks.explain: A correct slow solution on the board beats a blank editor; optimization then has a baseline.

choices: 1 − SLO: the allowed failure rate, spent deliberately on releases and risk
mockTasks.explain: 99.9% SLO → 0.1% budget: reliability as a spendable resource balancing velocity and stability.

mockTasks.q: Promoting the same immutable artifact through environments ensures:
choices: What you tested is what you ship — no rebuild skew between staging and prod
mockTasks.explain: Rebuilding per environment invalidates testing; immutable artifacts preserve it.

mockTasks.q: Under shared responsibility, an open S3 bucket is:
choices: The customer’s fault — data access control is in the customer’s layer
mockTasks.explain: The provider secures the service; you configure who can read your objects.

mockTasks.q: The root fix for XSS is:
choices: Context-appropriate output encoding of untrusted data (+ CSP in depth)
mockTasks.explain: XSS is code/data confusion in the browser; encoding keeps untrusted data as data.

mockTasks.q: Speed reps should always include stating complexity aloud because:
choices: The interview grades the analysis as well as the code — rehearse both together
mockTasks.explain: Rehearsing code without narration trains half the interview.

mockTasks.q: An ML system design that only covers the model is weak because:
choices: Production value lives in data, serving, and monitoring — the model is one piece
mockTasks.explain: Most ML failures are systems failures: skew, drift, latency — not the algorithm.

mockTasks.q: Enforcing policy at plan time (vs after deploy) is better because:
choices: Violations are blocked before they exist — prevention beats detection
mockTasks.explain: Shift-left for governance: the bad change never reaches the cloud.

choices: Allowed/rejected IP traffic metadata — who tried to reach whom
mockTasks.explain: Flow logs are the packet-level audit trail for security-group and routing diagnosis.

mockTasks.q: Wireshark showing repeated TCP retransmissions indicates:
choices: Packet loss or an unresponsive peer — a network-path problem, not application logic
mockTasks.explain: Retransmits are the transport layer saying ‘my packets aren’t getting through.’

mockTasks.q: Labeling arrows with what flows matters because:
choices: Unlabeled arrows hide the data story — the labels are where the design lives
mockTasks.explain: Architecture is data in motion; unlabeled arrows are just boxes.

choices: Removing blame gets honest timelines — people report what really happened
mockTasks.explain: Honest data requires psychological safety; blame produces cover stories instead of root causes.

mockTasks.q: The primary defense against drift is:
choices: Everything through code + scheduled plan/detect cycles
mockTasks.explain: If all changes flow through IaC, reality can’t silently diverge.

mockTasks.q: VPC peering is preferred over public IPs for inter-VPC traffic because:
choices: Traffic stays on the private backbone — no internet exposure
mockTasks.explain: Private routing beats public routing for both security and latency.

blocks.body: **SLI** = measured ratio (good events / total). **SLO** = target on the SLI (99.9% / 30d). **Error budget** = 1 − SLO. **Burn rate** = budget consumption speed vs the SLO window.
Allowed failures = total requests × (1 − SLO). Consumed % = failed ÷ allowed × 100. 99.9% over 1M requests → 1,000 allowed failures. Exhausted budget → freeze risky releases.
Fast-burn: page (multiwindow, e.g. 1h + 5m at 14x). Slow-burn: ticket. Alert on **symptoms** (burn rate, golden signals), never on causes.
Latency, traffic, errors, saturation. **USE** for resources (Utilization, Saturation, Errors). **RED** for services (Rate, Errors, Duration).

**Pod** (smallest unit) → **Deployment** (replicas + rolling updates) → **Service** (stable DNS/LB) → **Ingress** (external HTTP routing). **ConfigMap/Secret** for config; never bake config into images.
**CrashLoopBackOff** — container can’t stay alive (bad cmd/config/probe). **ImagePullBackOff** — registry/auth. **OOMKilled** — limits vs reality. **Pending** — no schedulable node.

- `kubectl get pods` — what’s happening
- `kubectl describe` — events narrate
- `kubectl logs --previous` — why it died
- `kubectl top` — resource pressure
- `rollout history` — what changed

kubectl describe pod <pod> -n prod
kubectl logs <pod> -n prod --previous --tail=100
kubectl top pods -n prod -l app=api

blocks.body: **IC**: decides, coordinates — doesn’t debug. **Comms**: status updates. **Scribe**: timeline. **SMEs**: debug.
Detect → respond (declare, assemble) → **mitigate first** → resolve → blameless postmortem. Mitigation before root cause, always.
One channel (#incident), every ~15 min even with ‘no update’, impact-first: who’s affected, what we’re doing, when’s next.
Blameless. Timeline, plural root causes (five whys with evidence), action items **with owners and dates**. The action items are the product.
Hypothesis → test → observe → update — **said out loud**. Time-box each hypothesis; narrate what each command tests.
DNS resolves? → TCP connects? → TLS handshakes? → HTTP responds? Each layer’s test isolates the fault.

openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443

cheatSheets.title: Reliability math — SLIs, SLOs, error budgets

blocks.body: SLI: the measurement (success ratio, p99 latency). SLO: the target (99.9% over 30d). SLA: the contract with consequences.
How fast you're consuming budget vs. time elapsed. Alert on fast burn (paging) vs slow burn (ticket). Multi-window alerts avoid flapping.
Budget remaining → ship. Budget exhausted → reliability work only. Blameless postmortems with owned action items.
Incident commander (coordinates), comms lead (status), ops (fixes), scribe (timeline). Commander doesn't type fixes.
Impact → scope → recent changes → mitigate (rollback/feature-flag/scale) → then root-cause. Mitigation beats diagnosis under pressure.
Status page updates every 15–30 min: what's broken, who's affected, what you're doing, next update time. Internal + external channels.
Blameless: timeline, contributing factors (never 'human error'), action items with owners and dates. Publish widely.
'Traffic flows LB → app → cache → DB. Latency spiked at the app tier, so I suspect...' — interviewers score the mental model, not just the fix.
Halve the system: is it app or data? Which tier? Which deploy? Binary search the blast radius.
'What changed?' — deploys, config, traffic, certs, cron. Most incidents are caused by a change; find it.
Metrics → logs → traces → repro. Each step narrows. State what would falsify your current hypothesis.

answerBank.q: What is an SLO, and why does the error budget matter?
answerBank.a: An SLO is a target on a measured indicator — e.g. 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days. The error budget (1 − SLO) turns reliability into arithmetic: budget remaining means ship freely; budget exhausted means freeze risky changes. It replaces arguments about ‘reliable enough’ with a number both product and engineering agree on, and burn-rate alerting pages us only when the objective is actually at risk.

answerBank.q: Walk me through your incident response.
answerBank.a: Declare the incident and assume command — the IC coordinates, doesn’t debug. Open the bridge and #incident, assign comms and scribe. Mitigate first (rollback, shed load), understand second. Comms go out every ~15 minutes, impact-first. Afterward: blameless postmortem with a timeline, plural root causes from evidence, and action items with owners and dates — because the action items are the actual product.

answerBank.q: How would you design a canary deployment?
answerBank.a: Ship the new version to a small percentage first, with automated promotion gated on error-rate and latency comparisons against the baseline — and automated rollback on breach. I’d keep the previous immutable artifact one command away, make DB migrations backward-compatible via expand-contract, and rehearse the rollback. Canary bounds the blast radius: problems meet 1% of users before 100%.

answerBank.q: Latency just spiked. How do you troubleshoot it live?
answerBank.a: Hypothesis-driven and narrated: check the four golden signals to scope it (which service, which endpoints via RED), correlate with deploy annotations — ‘what changed?’ is the first question — then bisect: is it downstream, the data layer (slow queries, pool exhaustion), or resource saturation (USE)? Each command tests one hypothesis; I time-box and update out loud rather than guessing silently.

answerBank.q: Blue-green vs canary vs rolling — how do you choose?
answerBank.a: By blast-radius tolerance and cost. Blue-green: instant cutover and rollback, but double capacity. Canary: safest for risky user-facing changes — progressive exposure with metric gates. Rolling: simplest, slowest rollback. I’d default to canary for the user-facing API, and I always name the rollback story for whichever I pick — a strategy without a rollback plan is a hope.

answerBank.q: How would you secure a cloud account from scratch?
answerBank.a: Identity first: SSO federation, no long-lived keys, workload roles, least-privilege policies with no wildcards. Guardrails: SCPs blocking the dangerous actions, Config rules detective. Data: KMS encryption at rest, TLS everywhere, secrets in a manager — never in repos or images. Logging: CloudTrail on with an audit trail nobody can quietly disable. Then policy-as-code so the guardrails are compiler errors, not wiki pages.

answerBank.q: Tell me about an outage you handled.
answerBank.a: STAR with SRE texture: the stakes fast (what was down, who was affected), the investigation as hypotheses tested — including the wrong call I made and what it cost — and the landing as a changed practice: what went into the runbook and the evidence it stuck. I keep it blameless and systems-focused; the lesson with proof is the whole point of the story.

glossary.definition: Service Level Indicator: the measured quantity (e.g., proportion of successful requests).
Service Level Objective: target SLI value over a window (99.9% / 30d).
1 − SLO: the allowed unreliability, spent on velocity or conserved for stability.
Rate of error-budget consumption relative to elapsed time; basis for paging vs ticket alerts.
Incident review focused on systemic causes and action items, never individual blame.
The coordinator role in incident response: runs the process, doesn't type the fix.
Manual repetitive ops work; SRE caps it and automates the remainder.
Monitoring methods: RED (Rate, Errors, Duration) for services; USE (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) for resources.
Releasing to a small traffic fraction first, promoting on health signals.
Runtime toggle decoupling deploy from release; the fastest incident mitigation lever.
Step-by-step operational procedure for a known failure mode — tested, not aspirational.
Practiced failure injection (chaos engineering lite) to validate runbooks and response.

faq.q: SRE vs DevOps — what's the interview distinction?
faq.a: DevOps: culture + CI/CD + automation practices. SRE: DevOps' engineering discipline with SLOs, error budgets, and toil caps. Interviewers want you to use the terms precisely.

faq.q: How do I answer 'tell me about a time you caused an outage'?
faq.a: Own it with the postmortem structure: impact, timeline, your actions, contributing factors, what changed (with owners). Blameless framing shows seniority.
Mental model stated → hypothesis → bisect by evidence → change correlation → mitigation before root cause → verification. Narrate every step aloud.

faq.q: Do I need to memorize the budget table?
faq.a: Know 99.9% (43m) and 99.99% (4.4m) cold; derive the rest. Interviewers test whether you can *use* the budget in a policy discussion.

faq.q: How technical should the security portion go?
faq.a: App/network/crypto fundamentals plus pipeline supply-chain security. You're interviewing as a defender who ships, not as a pentester.
Full timed loops: DSA speed reps, system-design reps, troubleshooting narration, behavioral — scored against rubrics, with weak-spot triage between rounds.

tips: Follow the guided path in order — each module unlocks the next. The sequence is the curriculum; skipping ahead breaks the chain.

This course maps to Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) and AWS Certified DevOps Engineer – Professional (DOP-C02) (independent preparation — no affiliation). Weight your drill time toward the heaviest exam domains shown in the cert gates.
The math modules (Probability & Statistics, Logic & Boolean Algebra, Cryptography in Practice) are load-bearing — finish them before the applied modules that assume them.
Quiz-gated modules need 70%+ to unlock the next. When you miss a question, ask Noah to walk you through the miss Socratically before re-attempting.
Do each hands-on lab twice — once following the guide, once from a blank screen. The second pass is where the skill sticks.
This is a 178-hour course: at 10 focused hours a week it takes about 4 months. Short daily sessions beat weekend cramming — pace it like a semester.

noahTutoring.tagline: Noah is the learning driver — not a bolt-on.
noahTutoring.concept: Noah is the core learning driver of IL-14 — the senior engineer across the table. Mentor runs incident-command scenarios and full interview loops by voice; Engineer makes you narrate troubleshooting aloud until the method is muscle memory. Reliability is a performance discipline, and Noah is the audience that never gets tired.

personas.label: Visionary
personas.style: Cuts to the fundamental truth, then projects forward. Challenges assumptions; frames everything as 'what could be.'

personas.label: Engineer
personas.style: Thinks in systems: inputs, outputs, constraints, failure modes. Concrete and actionable; quantifies; calls out trade-offs explicitly.

personas.label: Philosopher
personas.style: Asks the question beneath the question. Never rushes to answers; dwells in inquiry; repairs mental models with graduated hints.

personas.label: Mentor
personas.style: Notices effort and names it. Honest about difficulty; balances challenge with support; speaks like someone who has been where the learner is.

personas.label: Trickster
personas.style: Finds the absurd angle and the unexpected connection. Uses humor to illuminate; breaks fixation when the learner is stuck; kind, never punching down.

modulePersonaMap.why: Mentor runs the full loop by voice: incident-command scenarios under the clock, then a rubric debrief. The behavioral story bank gets STAR coaching — specific, honest, tight.
Engineer narrates troubleshooting aloud with a repeatable method: symptoms, hypotheses, cheapest test first. Quantifies everything — error budgets, blast radius, MTTR.
Philosopher asks the question beneath the design: what invariant must hold, what assumption are you smuggling in — the Socratic layer behind reliable systems.
Trickster asks 'what breaks at 3am on a holiday' — the lateral failure modes that separate operators who have lived it from those who have read about it.
Visionary stretches capacity planning to 10x: first-principles scaling, the economics of reliability, where the architecture wants to go.

voiceFirst.description: Talk with Noah via voice chat while working through modules — 5 distinct natural voices served by POST /api/noah/tts (Scholar, Narrator, Guide, Sage, Spark), plus adaptive browser speech: per-persona rate/pitch, emotion-aware delivery, lip-synced avatar. Voice-first mock interviews are the signature experience: Mentor asks, the clock runs, you answer aloud — exactly like the real loop.

adaptive.description: Review timing adapts to recall performance (docs/assets/noah-adaptive.js): quiz and drill results feed per-card intervals, so weak cards resurface sooner and mastered cards fade to maintenance. Mastery is tracked in localStorage; Noah re-sequences your next session around what is due, not what is next in the list.

courseAware.description: Noah tutors from this course's own knowledge — its answers are grounded in these modules, not generic web knowledge. If the endpoint is unreachable it degrades to a local Socratic engine with a plain notice. It never invents facts, credentials, or experience.

noahTutoring.houseRule: Bring Noah your hypothesis — not 'just give me the answer.' Attempt a card first.

multicloudLabs.brief: Design (on paper, then in the consoles) a pipeline that builds one golden image and replicates it to AWS (AMI), Azure (managed image), and GCP (custom image). Compare the replication primitives each cloud offers and where the design leaks. Adapted for IL-14 (interview track).

studyGuide.title: Study guide: how to work IL-14 in 8 weeks
pacing: Weeks 1-2 — Math + SRE, modules 1-8 (~46h): probability, logic, SLIs/SLOs, incident command, monitoring, capacity planning, SRE design reps, SRE mock circuit.
Weeks 3-4 — DevOps, modules 9-14 (~35h): CI/CD systems, IaC patterns, containers/orchestration, troubleshooting under pressure, guided platform build, DevOps mock.

Weeks 5-6 — Cloud + Security, modules 15-26 (~69h): cloud concepts, networking, data services, security controls, guided cloud architecture, cloud mock; then appsec, network security, crypto, detection/response, secure design review, security mock.

Weeks 7-8 — Full mock circuit, modules 27-31 (~29h): DSA speed reps, system-design reps, behavioral story bank, domain deep dives, full-loop simulation. Two consecutive full-loop clears on different days before the real loop.
rules: Narrate troubleshooting aloud from day one — the method is the skill.
Incident-command reps are timed; the clock is part of the training.
Quantify every answer: error budgets, blast radius, MTTR, cost.
Drills to green before the next module; re-take any quiz below 80%.
Bring Noah your hypothesis first — attempt every card before asking.
studyGuide.note: Totals are computed from module estimatedMinutes; pacing assumes ~25-30 focused hours per week.
